Lecture 7: Pandas¶

Laboratory: Coding - Accounting, Finance and Business Consulting¶

Introduction to Pandas: Data Manipulation and Analysis¶

  • Pandas: Built on top of NumPy, it is the go-to library for data manipulation and analysis in Python
    • Introduces data structures like Series and DataFrame (built on top of NumPy arrays) and eases data manipulation
  • Name Referring to both "Panel Data", and "Python Data Analysis"
    • Created by Wes McKinney in 2008 (of the reference book "Python for Data Analysis")

Pandas: Data Manipulation Made Easy - Crucial Functionalities¶

  • Crucial Functionalities:
    • Simplifies the process of grouping data and applying functions to each group
    • Automatic alignment of data based on labels, not just indices
      • Can manipulate measures of the same observation from different objects seamlessly
        • Pandas aligns them by index label (row name) automatically
    • Provides methods to handle missing data easily and effectively
    • Plotting methods perfectly integrate with Pandas data structures (especially Searborn)

Pandas: Data Manipulation Made Easy - More Functionalities¶

  • More Functionalities (we only touch them):
    • Allows more than one level of indexing: Hierarchical Indexing
      • Time series have a hirarchical index observation-time
    • Combinining datasets using merge and join operations
    • Fast and easy Input/Output functionalities: reading and writing data in different formats (CSV, Excel, SQL, etc.)

Pandas¶

  • Central tool for data cleaning and analysis in Python
  • Often used alongside NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, scikit-learn, and seaborn/matplotlib
  • Adopts NumPy's array-based computing style
    • Focuses on data processing without the need for iteration
  • Pandas vs. NumPy: Key Differences
    • Pandas is designed for tabular or heterogeneous data
    • NumPy is best for homogeneously typed numerical array data
  • Focuses on two main data structures: Series and DataFrame.
    • Series is a one-dimensional array-like object
    • DataFrame is a two-dimensional array-like object

Pandas Basics¶

Series in Pandas¶

  • One-dimensional array-like object
    • Contains a sequence of values and an associated array of data labels called index
  • Values must be of the same type
  • Index labels can be a (possibly non-sequential) integer sequence or a string sequence
    • Index allows to reference values in the Series
    • One of the most important features of Pandas
      • Makes it easy to perform operations based on index labels
      • E.g., group operations, align data of different objects for computation or merging

Series in Pandas¶

In [1]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
ser1 = pd.Series([4, 7, -5, 3]) 
ser2 = pd.Series([4, 7, -5, 3], index=['d', 'b', 'a', 'c'])
print(f"ser1 = pd.Series([4, 7, -5, 3]) creates a Series with default index: \n{ser1}\n")
print(f"ser2 = pd.Series([4, 7, -5, 3], index=['d', 'b', 'a', 'c']) creates a Series with custom index: \n{ser2}")

ser1 = pd.Series([4, 7, -5, 3]) creates a Series with default index: 
0    4
1    7
2   -5
3    3
dtype: int64

ser2 = pd.Series([4, 7, -5, 3], index=['d', 'b', 'a', 'c']) creates a Series with custom index: 
d    4
b    7
a   -5
c    3
dtype: int64

Index Updating¶

  • The index of an existing Series can be modified by assignment
    • series.index = new_index
    • New index must have the same length as the old one
      • Usually a list of ordered values or a transformation of the old index

Index Updating¶

In [2]:
print(f"ser2 is \n{ser2}")
ser2.index = ["D", "B", "A", "C"]
print(f'ser2.index = ["D", "B", "A", "C"] changes the index to uppercase: \n{ser2}')
ser2.index = ser2.index.str.lower()
print(f'ser2.index = ser2.index.str.lower() changes the index back to lowercase by applying the str.lower method: \n{ser2}')

ser2 is 
d    4
b    7
a   -5
c    3
dtype: int64

ser2.index = ser2.index.str.lower() changes the index back to lowercase by applying the str.lower method:

ser2["d"] = 6
print(f'ser2["d"] = 6 updates the value at label "d": \n{ser2}')

 d    4

-5

Indexing in Pandas Series¶

  • You can also specify a set of values to be selected
    • Expressed as a list of strings
In [4]:
print(f'ser2[["c", "a", "d"]] selects multiple values using a list of labels: \n{ser2[["c", "a", "d"]]}')

You can assign a name to the Series and its index to make it more readable

  • Numpy Operations like filtering and Numpy Ufuncs also work on Series
    • The index-value link is unaffected by these operations

print(f'ser2[ser2 > 0] filters values greater than zero: \n{ser2[ser2 > 0]}')
print(f'np.exp(ser2) applies the exponential function: \n{np.exp(ser2)}')

ser2[ser2 > 0] filters values greater than zero: 
state

a       0.006738

DataFrame in Pandas¶

Pandas DataFrames:

  • Represent rectangular table of data
    • Contains ordered, named collection of columns
      • A column is a named Series
      • Different columns may be of different data types
      • The type of the elements in each column is the same
  • Have both row and column indexes
    • Row indexes are called index
    • Column indexes are called column

DataFrame Creation¶

  • Based on dictionary structure
    • Each dictionary key is a column name
    • Each dictionary value is a column of data
  • Values needs to be of equal-length lists, 1D Numpy arrays, Pandas Series

DataFrame Creation¶

In [7]:
dict_data = {
    "state": ["Ohio", "Ohio", "Ohio", "Nevada", "Nevada", "Nevada"],
    "year": [2000, 2001, 2002, 2001, 2002, 2003],
    "pop": [1500000, 1700000, 3600000, 2400000, 2900000, 3200000]
}
df1 = pd.DataFrame(dict_data)
print(f'We want to use the data in dict_data :\ndata = {dict_data}\n')
print(f'Using: df1 = pd.DataFrame(dict_data) we create a DataFrame based on the dictionary: \n{df1}')

We want to use the data in dict_data :
data = {'state': ['Ohio', 'Ohio', 'Ohio', 'Nevada', 'Nevada', 'Nevada'], 'year': [2000, 2001, 2002, 2001, 2002, 2003], 'pop': [1500000, 1700000, 3600000, 2400000, 2900000, 3200000]}

Using: df1 = pd.DataFrame(dict_data) we create a DataFrame based on the dictionary: 
    state  year      pop
0    Ohio  2000  1500000
1    Ohio  2001  1700000
2    Ohio  2002  3600000
3  Nevada  2001  2400000
4  Nevada  2002  2900000
5  Nevada  2003  3200000

Pandas Data Types¶

  • Pandas DataFrames are versatile and can hold a variety of data types (most of Numpy and more)
  • Each column in a DataFrame can have its own data type
    • Use df.dtypes to view the data type of each column in a DataFrame
    • Use df['column_name'].dtype to view the data type of a single column in a DataFrame
    • Use astype() to convert to a given data type (the usual caveats/warnings apply)

DataFrame Index and Column Ordering¶

  • Columns are ordered based on the key order in the dictionary
    • You can order the columns by specifying it to the columns parameter
    • If you pass a column that isn't in the dictionary, it will appear with missing values
  • The index is automatically assigned, similar to Series
    • The DataFrame df will have its index starting from 0 and incrementing by 1
    • You can specify the index by passing a list to the index parameter or modify it using the index method

DataFrame Index and Column Ordering¶

In [8]:
df2 = pd.DataFrame(dict_data, columns=["year", "state", "pop", "debt"])
print(f'''df2 = pd.DataFrame(dict_data, columns=["year", "state", "pop", "debt"]) constructs a 
DataFrame with specified column order and an additional "debt" column (with all NaN since no data about it is available): \n{df2}\n''')
df2.index = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']# Changing the index to string labels
print(f'The command df2.index = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"] changes the index to string labels: \n{df2}')

df2 = pd.DataFrame(dict_data, columns=["year", "state", "pop", "debt"]) constructs a 
DataFrame with specified column order and an additional "debt" column (with all NaN since no data about it is available): 
   year   state      pop debt
0  2000    Ohio  1500000  NaN
1  2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
2  2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
3  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN
4  2002  Nevada  2900000  NaN
5  2003  Nevada  3200000  NaN

The command df2.index = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"] changes the index to string labels:

d  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN

DataFrame Using a Column as Index - The set_index Method¶

  • You can use the set_index method to create a new index based on a column
    • The column will be removed from the DataFrame
  • This creates a new DataFrame object, does not modify the original one
In [9]:
print(f"The command df2.set_index('year') creates a new dataFrame using 'year' as the index and removes it from the columns: \n{df2.set_index('year')}\n")
print(f"df2 is still \n{df2}\n")

The command df2.set_index('year') creates a new dataFrame using 'year' as the index and removes it from the columns: 
       state      pop debt
year                      
2000    Ohio  1500000  NaN
2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN
2002  Nevada  2900000  NaN
2003  Nevada  3200000  NaN

df2 is still 
   year   state      pop debt
a  2000    Ohio  1500000  NaN
b  2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
c  2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
d  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN
e  2002  Nevada  2900000  NaN
f  2003  Nevada  3200000  NaN

DataFrame Using a Column as Index - The set_index Method - The drop Parameter¶

  • The index is separate from the columns, so it is less convenient to access
    • Some variables are useful to use both as index and for computations
    • Time is often needed to identify observations, but also needed to compute obs age or distance from an event
  • Use the drop parameter to keep the column in the DataFrame
In [10]:
print(f"The command df2.set_index('year', drop=False)) creates a new dataFrame using 'state' as the index and removes it from the columns: \n{df2.set_index('year', drop=False)}\n")

The command df2.set_index('year', drop=False)) creates a new dataFrame using 'state' as the index and removes it from the columns: 
      year   state      pop debt
year                            
2000  2000    Ohio  1500000  NaN
2001  2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
2002  2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
2001  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN
2002  2002  Nevada  2900000  NaN
2003  2003  Nevada  3200000  NaN

DataFrame Using a Column as Index - The set_index Method - The inplace Parameter¶

  • Using the parameter inplace=True will modify the DataFrame in place
    • This is a functionality available in many Pandas methods
In [11]:
df2.set_index('year', drop=False, inplace=True)
print(f"The command df2.set_index('year', drop=False, inplace=True) updates df2 setting 'year' as the index and keeps it among the columns: \n{df2}\n")

The command df2.set_index('year', drop=False, inplace=True) updates df2 setting 'year' as the index and keeps it among the columns: 
      year   state      pop debt
year                            
2000  2000    Ohio  1500000  NaN
2001  2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
2002  2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
2001  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN
2002  2002  Nevada  2900000  NaN
2003  2003  Nevada  3200000  NaN

DataFrame Using a Column as Index - The reset_index Method¶

  • The reset_index method does the opposite of set_index
    • It takes the index and makes it a column in the DataFrame
  • The index is then reset to the default integer index
In [12]:
print(f"The command df2.set_index('state').reset_index() retrieves 'state' back from the index into the DataFrame: \n{df2.set_index('year').reset_index()}\n")
df2.index = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']
print(f"""Using df2.index = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f'] we get to the original form of df2 : \n{df2}\n""")

The command df2.set_index('state').reset_index() retrieves 'state' back from the index into the DataFrame: 
   year   state      pop debt
0  2000    Ohio  1500000  NaN
1  2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
2  2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
3  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN
4  2002  Nevada  2900000  NaN
5  2003  Nevada  3200000  NaN

Using df2.index = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f'] we get to the original form of df2 :

b  2001    Ohio  1700000  NaN
c  2002    Ohio  3600000  NaN
d  2001  Nevada  2400000  NaN

Using Hierarchical Indexing for Multi-Dimensional Data¶

  • Pandas dataFrames are inherently two-dimensional
    • Usually in a tidy dataset we:
      • Store different measures - in the column dimension
      • For different observations - in the row dimension
  • In real-world scenarios, data can be three-dimensional or higher:
    • E.g., panel data contains three dimensions: observations (row), measures (column), and time (?)
      • Numpy address this problem with 3D arrays (from MatLab)
  • Hierarchical indexing provides a way to represent multi-dimensional data within the two-dimensional structure of a DataFrame
    • This feature allows to have multiple index levels on an axis
    • Capturing the complexity of panel data or higher-dimensional data

Defining a MultiIndex on Existing DataFrames¶

  • Just pass to the set_index method multiple column names
In [13]:
print(f"df1 is: \n{df1}\n")
df1.set_index(['state', 'year'], inplace=True)
print(f"The command df1.set_index(['state', 'year'], inplace=True) set a MultiIndex (state, year): \n{df1}\n")

df1 is: 
    state  year      pop
0    Ohio  2000  1500000
1    Ohio  2001  1700000
2    Ohio  2002  3600000
3  Nevada  2001  2400000
4  Nevada  2002  2900000
5  Nevada  2003  3200000

The command df1.set_index(['state', 'year'], inplace=True) set a MultiIndex (state, year): 
                 pop
state  year         
Ohio   2000  1500000
       2001  1700000
       2002  3600000
Nevada 2001  2400000
       2002  2900000
       2003  3200000

MultiIndexing Resources¶

  • Multindexing is sometimes crucial for data manipulation and analysis using external libraries
    • statsmodels, scikit-learn
  • We won't cover it in detail, here you can find more resources:
    • Python Data Science Handbook 03.05
    • MultiIndexing tutorial by Datacamp

Accessing Columns in Pandas DataFrame¶

  • Multiple ways to access columns for flexibility and convenience

  • Bracket Notation

    • Use brackets and
      • Specify the column name as a string
      • Specify the column names as a list of strings
    • Works for any column name, even those with spaces or special characters

Accessing Columns in Pandas DataFrame - Bracket Notation¶

In [14]:
print(f'df2["year"] accesses the "year" column using bracket notation: \n{df2["year"]}')
print(f'df2[["year", "state"]] accesses the "year" and "state" columns using bracket notation: \n{df2[["year", "state"]]}')

df2["year"] accesses the "year" column using bracket notation: 
a    2000
b    2001
c    2002
d    2001
e    2002
f    2003
Name: year, dtype: int64
df2[["year", "state"]] accesses the "year" and "state" columns using bracket notation: 
   year   state
a  2000    Ohio
b  2001    Ohio
c  2002    Ohio
d  2001  Nevada
e  2002  Nevada
f  2003  Nevada

Accessing Columns in Pandas DataFrame - Attribute/Method Notation¶

  • Multiple ways to access columns for flexibility and convenience

  • Attribute/Method notation

    • Use dot notation, similar to attribute access in Python objects
    • I.e., df2.year accesses the "year" column
    • Column name can be retrieved using Tab completion
      • But can retrieve just one column at time
    • Only works for valid Python variable names and non-conflicting DataFrame methods

Accessing Columns in Pandas DataFrame - Attribute/Method Notation¶

In [15]:
print(f'df2.year accesses the "year" column using dot notation: \n{df2.year}')

df2.year accesses the "year" column using dot notation: 
a    2000
b    2001
c    2002
d    2001
e    2002
f    2003
Name: year, dtype: int64

Column Creation in Pandas DataFrame¶

  • Direct Assignment
    • Assign a scalar value or an array-like object to a new column
    • Using Lists or Arrays
      • Use a list to populate a new column. The list length must match the DataFrame length
    • Using Series
      • Index labels of the series are matched to the DataFrame's index
  • Derived Columns
    • Create new columns resulting from computations on existing ones

Column Creation in Pandas DataFrame - Direct Assignment Using a Scalar Value¶

In [16]:
df2["debt"] = 2e9
print(f'df2["debt"] = 2e9 adds a new column "debt" with the scalar of 2 billions: \n{df2}')
df2["country"] = "USA"
print(f'df2["country"] = "USA" adds a new column "country" with a string value "USA": \n{df2}')

df2["debt"] = 2e9 adds a new column "debt" with the scalar of 2 billions:

d  2001  Nevada  2400000  2.000000e+09
e  2002  Nevada  2900000  2.000000e+09
f  2003  Nevada  3200000  2.000000e+09

b  2001    Ohio  1700000  2.000000e+09     USA
c  2002    Ohio  3600000  2.000000e+09     USA

Column Creation in Pandas DataFrame - Direct Assignment Using Lists or Arrays¶

  • Using Lists or Arrays: Use a list to populate a new column
    • The list length must match the DataFrame length
In [17]:
# Creating a list of values
debt_values = [1.2e9, 1.5e9, 1.7e9, 0.5e9, 0.8e9, 1.0e9]
print(f'debt_values = [1.2e9, 1.5e9, 1.7e9, 0.5e9, 0.8e9, 1.0e9] creates a list of values: \n{debt_values}\n')
df2["debt"] = debt_values
print(f'df2["debt"] = debt_values assigns the list to the "debt" column in frame2: \n{df2}')

debt_values = [1.2e9, 1.5e9, 1.7e9, 0.5e9, 0.8e9, 1.0e9] creates a list of values: 
[1200000000.0, 1500000000.0, 1700000000.0, 500000000.0, 800000000.0, 1000000000.0]

df2["debt"] = debt_values assigns the list to the "debt" column in frame2: 
   year   state      pop          debt country
a  2000    Ohio  1500000  1.200000e+09     USA
b  2001    Ohio  1700000  1.500000e+09     USA
c  2002    Ohio  3600000  1.700000e+09     USA
d  2001  Nevada  2400000  5.000000e+08     USA
e  2002  Nevada  2900000  8.000000e+08     USA
f  2003  Nevada  3200000  1.000000e+09     USA

Column Creation in Pandas DataFrame - Direct Assignment Using Series¶

  • If you assign a Series to a DataFrame column, index labels are matched to the DataFrame's index
    • The Series index takes precedence on order in alignment
    • Any DataFrame index not present in the Series will have NaN in the new column

Column Creation in Pandas DataFrame - Direct Assignment Using Series - Matching Indexes¶

In [18]:
# Creating a new Series with specified index that matches the DataFrame's index
income_series = pd.Series([50.2e3, 45.3e3, 60.1e3, 55.5e3, 42.8e3, 38.9e3], index=['b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'a'])
print(f"""income_series = pd.Series([50.2e3, 45.3e3, 60.1e3, 55.5e3, 42.8e3, 38.9e3], index=['b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'a']) 
creates a new Series with specified index:\n{income_series}\n""")
df2["income"] = income_series # Assigning the Series to a DataFrame column
print(f'df2["income"] = income_series assigns the Series to the "income" column in df2, aligning by index: \n{df2}')

income_series = pd.Series([50.2e3, 45.3e3, 60.1e3, 55.5e3, 42.8e3, 38.9e3], index=['b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f', 'a']) 
creates a new Series with specified index:
b    50200.0
c    45300.0
d    60100.0
e    55500.0
f    42800.0
a    38900.0
dtype: float64

df2["income"] = income_series assigns the Series to the "income" column in df2, aligning by index: 
   year   state      pop          debt country   income

# Creating a new Series with specified index (not matching the one of the dataFrame)
val = pd.Series([2e3, 3e3, 4e3], index=['b', 'd', 'f'])
print(f"val = pd.Series([2e3, 3e3, 4e3], index=['b', 'd', 'f'] creates a new Series with specified index:\n{val}\n")
df2["income"] = val # Assigning the Series to a DataFrame column - notice that we overwrite ALL the previous values
print(f'df2["income"] = val assigns the Series to the "debt" column in frame2, aligning by index:\n{df2}')

Column Creation in Pandas DataFrame - Derived Columns¶

  • Derived Columns: Create new columns based on existing ones
    • The most common occurence
In [20]:
df2["per_capita_debt"] = df2["debt"] / df2["pop"] 
print(f'df2["per_capita_debt"] = df2["debt"] / df2["pop"] creates a new column "per_capita_debt" measuring per-capita debt: \n{df2}')

Row Retrieval in Pandas DataFrame - loc and iloc¶

  • Rows can be retrieved using loc and iloc methods
    • loc is label-based data selection
      • Need to specify the index label of the row to select
    • iloc is position-based data selection
      • Need to specify the position of the row to select
In [21]:

c  2002    Ohio  3600000  1.700000e+09     USA     NaN       472.222222

Row Retrieval in Pandas DataFrame - loc¶

  • loc is label-based data selection
    • Need to specify the index label of the row to select
In [22]:
print(f'df2.loc["b"] retrieves the row with index label "b": \n{df2.loc["b"]}\n')
print(f'df2.loc[["b", "c"]] retrieves the row with indexes label "b" and "c": \n{df2.loc[["b", "c"]]}')

per_capita_debt      882.352941

   year state      pop          debt country  income  per_capita_debt
b  2001  Ohio  1700000  1.500000e+09     USA  2000.0       882.352941
c  2002  Ohio  3600000  1.700000e+09     USA     NaN       472.222222

Row Retrieval in Pandas DataFrame - iloc¶

  • iloc is index-based data selection
    • Need to specify the position of the row to select

print(f'df2.iloc[1] retrieves the row with integer position 2, which corresponds to label "b": \n{df2.iloc[1]}\n')
print(f'df2.iloc[[1, 2]] retrieves the row with integer position 2 and 3, which correspond to label "b" and "c": \n{df2.iloc[[1, 2]]}')

Conditional Selection in DataFrames¶

  • Conditionals are used to filter rows based on specific criteria, same as Numpy
    • The conditional expression returns a Boolean Series

df2['year'] > 2001
print(f"df2['year'] > 2001 returns a Boolean Series: \n{df2['year'] > 2001}")

b    False
c     True
d    False
e     True

Name: year, dtype: bool

Conditional Selection in DataFrames¶

  • Conditionals are used to filter rows based on specific criteria, same as Numpy
    • The Boolean Series used in indexing selects rows with True and drops the False ones

Combining Row and Column Selection in Pandas¶

  • You can combine both row and column selection
    • In loc, you separate the label-based indexes of row and column with a comma
    • In iloc, you separate the integer-based indexing with a comma

Combining Row and Column Selection in Pandas¶

In [27]:
print(f'df2 is: \n{df2}\n')
print(f'''df2.loc[["a", "b"], ["year", "state", "pop"]] retrieves specific rows and columns by label:
{df2.loc[["a", "b"], ["year", "state", "pop"]]}\n''')
print(f'df2.iloc[[0, 1], [0, 1, 2]] retrieves specific rows and columns by index: \n{df2.iloc[[0, 1], [0, 1, 2]]}\n')

df2 is: 
   year   state      pop          debt country  income  per_capita_debt
a  2000    Ohio  1500000  1.200000e+09     USA     NaN       800.000000

c  2002    Ohio  3600000  1.700000e+09     USA     NaN       472.222222

a  2000  Ohio  1500000
b  2001  Ohio  1700000

df2.iloc[[0, 1], [0, 1, 2]] retrieves specific rows and columns by index: 
   year state      pop
a  2000  Ohio  1500000
b  2001  Ohio  1700000

Integer Indexing: Label-based vs Position-based¶

  • Do not use df[row_mask, col_mask] without .loc/.iloc, you will get errors

  • Chained indexing like df[rows][cols] can work for reading but is unsafe

  • In Pandas, using integers for indexing can be ambiguous

    • The cases where is unclear if label-based or position-based indexing should be applied
  • Pandas throws an error when there are ambiguities
  • It is recommended to be explicit using loc and iloc so to avoid confusion

Dropping Columns and Rows in Pandas - The drop Method¶

  • In a data analysis workflow, you often need to drop rows and columns
    • Observations not of interest
    • Intermediate columns no longer needed
  • The drop returns a new DataFrame without the selected rows/columns
    • The original DataFrame is not modified, but can be using inplace=True
  • drop accepts various parameters, my advice is to use:
    • columns: column name(s) to drop
    • index: Index label(s) to drop

Dropping Columns and Rows in Pandas - Dropping a Column¶

Pandas Operations and Methods¶

Pandas Built-in Methods¶

  • Pandas provides a variety of built-in methods for efficient computation of common statistics and data transformations

Table 5.8: Descriptive and Summary Statistics Methods in Pandas¶

There are many methods for computing descriptive and summary statistics on Series and DataFrame objects

Method Description
abs() Calculates the absolute value.
round() Rounds values to a specified number of decimal places.
count() Number of values.
value_counts() Returns a Series containing counts of unique values.
describe() Generates descriptive statistics.
mean() Computes the mean of the values.
median() Computes the median of the values.
min(), max() Finds the minimum/maximum value.
idxmin(), idxmax() Compute index labels of the minimum/maximum value
rank() Ranks the values within each column (different tie breaking rules can be chosen ).
std() Calculates the standard deviation.
var() Calculates the variance.
quantile() Computes the quantile of the values.
corr() Computes pairwise correlation of columns.
cov() Computes pairwise covariance of columns.
sum() Sums up the values.
prod() Calculates the product of the values.
diff() Calculates the change between the current and a prior element.
pct_change() Computes the percentage change between the current and a prior element.
cumsum() Cumulative sum of values.
cumprod() Cumulative product of values.
cummax() Cumulative maximum of values.
cummin() Cumulative minimum of values.

Pandas Built-in Methods - Column-wise and Row-wise Operations¶

  • These functions operate column-wise by default
    • Use axis="columns" to apply functions across rows
      • Examples:
        • df.sum(): Sum of values in each column.
        • df.sum(axis="columns"): Sum of values in each row

Exploring Built-in Methods in Pandas¶

In [31]:
df5 = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(12).reshape(4, 3), columns=['A', 'B', 'C'])
print(f"DataFrame df5:\n{df5}\n")
print(f"df5.sum() computes the sum of each column: \n{df5.sum()}\n")
print(f"df5.sum(axis='columns') computes the sum of each row: \n{df5.sum(axis='columns')}\n")
print(f"df5.sum(axis=1) computes the sum of each row: \n{df5.sum(axis=1)}\n")

DataFrame df5:
   A   B   C
0  0   1   2
1  3   4   5
2  6   7   8
3  9  10  11

df5.sum() computes the sum of each column: 
A    18
B    22
C    26
dtype: int64

df5.sum(axis='columns') computes the sum of each row: 
0     3
1    12
2    21
3    30
dtype: int64

df5.sum(axis=1) computes the sum of each row: 
0     3
1    12
2    21
3    30
dtype: int64

Pandas Built-in Methods - NaN Handling¶

  • Pandas Built-in Methods automatically handle NaN in computations
    • Missing values are substitute witha a "reasonable" value
In [32]:
df6 = pd.DataFrame([[1.4, np.nan], [7.1, -4.5], [np.nan, np.nan]],
                  index=["a", "b", "c"],
                  columns=["one", "two"])
print(f"df6 is: \n{df6}\n")
print(f"df6.sum(axis='columns') calculates the sum of each row: \n{df6.sum(axis='columns')}\n")
print(f"df6.mean(axis='columns') calculates the mean of each row: \n{df6.mean(axis='columns')}\n")

df6 is: 
   one  two
a  1.4  NaN
b  7.1 -4.5
c  NaN  NaN

df6.sum(axis='columns') calculates the sum of each row: 
a    1.4
b    2.6
c    0.0
dtype: float64

df6.mean(axis='columns') calculates the mean of each row: 
a    1.4
b    1.3
c    NaN
dtype: float64

  • Missing values exclusion can be disabled by setting skipna = False

print(f"df6 is: \n{df6}\n")
print(f"df6.sum(axis='columns', skipna=False) calculates the sum of each row, including NaN: \n{df6.sum(axis='columns', skipna=False)}\n")
print(f"df6.mean(axis='columns', skipna=False) calculates the mean of each row, including NaN: \n{df6.mean(axis='columns', skipna=False)}")

df6 is: 
   one  two
a  1.4  NaN
b  7.1 -4.5
c  NaN  NaN

df6.sum(axis='columns', skipna=False) calculates the sum of each row, including NaN: 
a    NaN
b    2.6
c    NaN
dtype: float64

df6.mean(axis='columns', skipna=False) calculates the mean of each row, including NaN: 
a    NaN
b    1.3
c    NaN
dtype: float64

Some Examples of Pandas Methods - describe¶

  • The describe method computes multiple summary statistics by column
    • Using it on a DataFrame with mixed data types applies it just to numeric columns

Some Examples of Pandas Methods - describe¶

In [34]:

print(f"df7.describe produces the following output:\n{df7.describe()}\n")

Some Examples of Pandas Methods - unique and value_counts¶

  • Knowing what are the unique values and their frequency is a crucial step in data cleaning and analysis
  • The unique method returns an array of unique values in a Series
  • The value_counts method computes a Series containing the frequency of each unique value

unique and value_counts on a Series¶

In [37]:
ser6 = pd.Series(["d", "a", np.NaN,  "a", "b", "b", np.NaN, "c"])
print(f"ser6 is: \n{ser6}\n")
print(f"ser6.unique() finds unique values: {ser6.unique()}\n")
print(f"ser6.value_counts(dropna=False) counts and the frequency of each unique value (including NaN): \n{ser6.value_counts(dropna=False)}\n")

ser6 is: 
0      d
1      a
2    NaN
3      a
4      b
5      b
6    NaN
7      c
dtype: object

ser6.unique() finds unique values: ['d' 'a' nan 'b' 'c']

ser6.value_counts(dropna=False) counts and the frequency of each unique value (including NaN): 
a      2
NaN    2
b      2
d      1
c      1
dtype: int64

unique and value_counts on a DataFrame Column¶

In [38]:

print(f"df2['income'].value_counts(dropna = False) counts the frequency of each unique value in the 'income' column (including NaN): \n{df2['income'].value_counts(dropna = False)}\n")

Numpy Ufuncs in Pandas¶

  • NumPy ufuncs work seamlessly with Pandas DataFrames
    • They apply element-wise to the entire DataFrame
    • Examples of ufuncs: np.abs, np.sqrt, np.exp, np.log
  • Example: Using np.abs() to get the absolute values of DataFrame elements

Numpy Ufuncs in Pandas¶

In [39]:
df5 = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(-6, 6).reshape(3, 4), columns=["a", "b", "c", "d"], index=["Utah", "Ohio", "Texas"])
print(f"df5 is: \n{df5}\n")
print(f"np.abs(df5) applies the absolute value function to each element of df5: \n{np.abs(df5)}\n")

       a  b  c  d
Utah  -6 -5 -4 -3
Ohio  -2 -1  0  1
Texas  2  3  4  5

np.abs(df5) applies the absolute value function to each element of df5: 
       a  b  c  d
Utah   6  5  4  3
Ohio   2  1  0  1
Texas  2  3  4  5

Sorting¶

Sorting¶

  • Sorted data allows to quickly identify patterns along with potential outliers/errors/missing values
    • E.g., you computed a measure of a given phenomena (mean height of children in a school) and:
      • You want to see how it varies across (groups of) observations
        • E.g., are there more females or males at the extremes?
      • Are there inexplicably tall or short children? have there been recording errors?
  • Ranking is just a special case of sorting
    • Assigns ranks from one through the number of valid data points in an array
    • The rank of a value is its index in the sorted array

Sorting to Present Analysis' Results¶

  • Apart from easen data exploration, sorting plays a major role in presenting analysis results
  • One of the most common way of presenting analysis results is by means of tables
    • Pandas Dataframe are already in a tabular format
      • That are rendered as fairly nice tables in Jupyter Notebooks
      • Can also be exported in a variety of tabular formats (e.g., excel)
  • A CRUCIAL aspect of a good presentation of result is its clarity
    • The information that you want to provide should be easily accessible to the reader
  • Sorting is the most basic prerequisite to make a table clear and easy to read

Sorting in Pandas¶

  • Sorting in Pandas can be done using the sort_index and sort_values methods
  • sort_index sorts the data lexicographically by index or column label
    • By default, sorting is done in ascending order. Use ascending=False for descending
  • sort_values sorts a pandas object by its values
    • Ascending takes a Boolean list to specify sorting order for each column
  • Both methods return a new, sorted object
    • The original object is not modified
    • Use inplace=True to modify the original object

Sorting Series - sort_index¶

In [40]:
print(f"ser2 series is: \n{ser2}\n")
print(f"ser2.sort_index() sorts by index: \n{ser2.sort_index()}\n")
print(f"ser2.sort_index(ascending=False) sorts by index in descending order: \n{ser2.sort_index(ascending=False)}\n")

Sorting DataFrames - sort_index¶

  • A DataFrame has two indexes (rows and columns)
    • The default behaviour is sort by row index (axis=0/axis='rows')
    • ascending=True sorts the index in ascending order

Sorting DataFrames - sort_values¶

  • Sorting a DataFrame by values needs to specify the column to sort by
    • by="column_name" specifies the column to sort by
    • by=["column_name1", "column_name2"] specifies multiple columns to sort by

print(f"df8.sort_values(['Age', 'Score'], ascending=[True, False]) sorts by columns 'Age' (ascending) and 'Score' (descending): \n{df8.sort_values(['Age', 'Score'], ascending=[True, False])}\n")

📊 Exercises: More Exercises on Pandas Methods¶

You have a Series representing various market sectors with some entries being repeated and others missing. Use the Series to answer the following questions:

  1. Identify Unique Sectors: Use the unique method to find all the unique market sectors in the Series.

  2. Frequency Count of Sectors: Apply the value_counts method to count the frequency of each sector, excluding the missing values.

  3. Include Missing Values in Count: Modify the previous task to include the count of missing (NaN) values using the value_counts method.

  4. Percentage Distribution of Sectors: Calculate the percentage distribution of each sector (including missing values) in the Series. Ensure that the percentages sum up to 100%.

Data:¶

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

market_sectors = pd.Series([
    "Technology", "Healthcare", "Energy", "Energy", "Manufacturing", np.NaN, "Agriculture",
    "Technology", np.NaN, "Retail", "Finance", None, "Energy", "Healthcare", 
    "Aerospace", "Retail", "Technology", "Agriculture", "Finance", "Manufacturing", 
    "Technology", "Energy", "Healthcare", np.NaN, "Finance", "Retail", "Energy", 
    "Agriculture", "Technology", np.NaN, "Retail", "Healthcare", None, "Manufacturing",
    "Technology", "Finance", "Retail", "Energy", "Agriculture", "Manufacturing", 
    None, "Aerospace", "Technology", "Retail", "Finance", np.NaN, "Energy", 
    "Agriculture", "Manufacturing", "Retail", "Technology", "Healthcare", "Finance"
])

Dealing with Missing Values and Duplicated Observations in Pandas¶

Missing Data¶

  • Missing data is a common issue in data analysis
  • Consists of non-existent or unobserved data
  • It is important to have a clear picture of missing data in the dataset under analysis:
    • Provides info of the representativeness of the data
    • Identifies potential biases that might invalidate the analysis
    • Might point towards data collection problems

Missing Data in Pandas - Values and Methods¶

Pandas aims to simplify dealing with missing data

  • There are two objects used as sentinel values for missing data:
    • NaN (Not a Number, from Numpy) to represent missing data for numeric values
    • None(from basic Python) to represent other missing data
    • This distinction is important for some operations, but these are mainly edge cases
  • Pandas provides methods to handle missing data:
    • isna (notna) returns a Boolean Series indicating which values are (not) missing

Identifying and Removing Missing Data¶

In [47]:
ser_nan = pd.Series([1.2, np.nan, None,  -3.5, 2, 0], index=["a", "b", np.nan, "d", np.nan, "f"])
print(f"The series ser_nan is:\n{ser_nan}\n")
print(f"The command ser_nan.isna() returns a boolean Series with True for NaN values: \n{ser_nan.isna()}\n")
print(f"The command ser_nan.isna().sum() easily computes the number of NaN values: \n{ser_nan.isna().sum()}\n")

The series ser_nan is:
a      1.2
b      NaN
NaN    NaN
d     -3.5
NaN    2.0
f      0.0
dtype: float64

The command ser_nan.isna() returns a boolean Series with True for NaN values: 
a      False
b       True
NaN     True
d      False
NaN    False
f      False
dtype: bool

The command ser_nan.isna().sum() easily computes the number of NaN values: 
2

Filtering Missing Data in Series¶

  • To Filter Missing Data:
    • Manual filtering using isna/notna and Boolean indexing
    • Automated approach using dropna method
  • dropna on a Series only return elements that have non-missing value
  • The inplace parameter allows to modify the Series in place

Filtering Missing Data in Series¶

In [48]:
print(f"The series ser_nan is:\n{ser_nan}\n")
print(f"The command ser_nan[ser_nan.notna()] returns it with NaN values removed: \n{ser_nan[ser_nan.notna()]}\n")
print(f"The command ser_nan.dropna() returns it with NaN values removed: \n{ser_nan.dropna()}\n")

The series ser_nan is:
a      1.2
b      NaN
NaN    NaN
d     -3.5
NaN    2.0
f      0.0
dtype: float64

The command ser_nan[ser_nan.notna()] returns it with NaN values removed: 
a      1.2
d     -3.5
NaN    2.0
f      0.0
dtype: float64

The command ser_nan.dropna() returns it with NaN values removed: 
a      1.2
d     -3.5
NaN    2.0
f      0.0
dtype: float64

Filtering Missing Data in DataFrames¶

  • Removing missing data in dataFrames offers more options:
    • axis={0,1} sets whether to drop rows or columns
    • how={any, all} sets whether to drop a row/column that have any/all NA
    • thresh sets the minimum number of non-NA values required to keep a row/column

Filtering Missing Data in DataFrames¶

In [49]:
df_nan = pd.DataFrame({'A': [4, 1, 3, np.nan],'B': [3, np.nan, 2, np.nan],'C': [3, np.nan, 1, np.nan],'D': [1, 2, np.nan, np.nan]})
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"The command df_nan.dropna() drops all rows with any NaN values: \n{df_nan.dropna()}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

The command df_nan.dropna() drops all rows with any NaN values: 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0

Filtering Missing Data in DataFrames¶

In [50]:
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"df_nan.dropna(axis=0, how='all') drops all rows with all NaN values: \n{df_nan.dropna(axis=0, how='all')}\n")
print(f"df_nan.dropna(axis=1, thresh=3) drops all columns with less than three non-NaN values: \n{df_nan.dropna(axis=1, thresh=3)}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

df_nan.dropna(axis=0, how='all') drops all rows with all NaN values: 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN

df_nan.dropna(axis=1, thresh=3) drops all columns with less than three non-NaN values: 
     A
0  4.0
1  1.0
2  3.0
3  NaN

Filling Missing Data in DataFrames¶

In some cases it is better to fill missing data instead of dropping them

  • fillna fills missings with a specific value
    • The mean and the median are used in many applications
  • Nearby (and thus possibly related) observations can be used to fill missing:
    • bfill uses backwards obs
    • ffill uses forward obs
    • interpolate interpolates obs
    • limit allows to limit the number of consecutive missing values that will be filled

Filling Missing Data in DataFrames - Fill with a Set Value: fillna¶

In [51]:
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"df_nan.fillna(0) fills all NaN values with 0: \n{df_nan.fillna(0)}\n")
print(f"df_nan.fillna(df_nan.mean()) fills all NaN values with the mean of the column: \n{df_nan.fillna(df_nan.mean())}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

df_nan.fillna(0) fills all NaN values with 0: 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  0.0  0.0  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  0.0
3  0.0  0.0  0.0  0.0

df_nan.fillna(df_nan.mean()) fills all NaN values with the mean of the column: 
          A    B    C    D
0  4.000000  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.000000  2.5  2.0  2.0
2  3.000000  2.0  1.0  1.5
3  2.666667  2.5  2.0  1.5

Filling Missing Data in DataFrames - Backward and Forward Filling: bfill and ffill¶

In [52]:
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"df_nan.ffill() forward-fills the first NaN value : \n{df_nan.ffill(limit=1)}\n")
print(f"df_nan.bfill() backward-fills all NaN values: \n{df_nan.bfill()}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

df_nan.ffill() forward-fills the first NaN value : 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  3.0  3.0  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  2.0
3  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN

df_nan.bfill() backward-fills all NaN values: 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  2.0  1.0  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

Filling Missing Data in DataFrames - Filling by interpolation: interpolate¶

  • If there are no backward values bfill is used
  • If there are no forward values ffill is used
In [53]:
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"df_nan.interpolate() interpolates NaN values: \n{df_nan.interpolate()}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

df_nan.interpolate() interpolates NaN values: 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  2.5  2.0  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  2.0
3  3.0  2.0  1.0  2.0

Filling Missing Data in DataFrames - the axis Parameter¶

  • The axis parameter allows to specify whether to fill by column (axis={0, rows}, default) or by row (axis={1, columns})
In [54]:
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"df_nan.ffill(limit=1, axis='columns') forward-fills the first NaN value by row: \n{df_nan.ffill(limit=1, axis='columns')}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

df_nan.ffill(limit=1, axis='columns') forward-fills the first NaN value by row: 
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  1.0  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  1.0
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

Filling Missing Data in DataFrames - the axis Parameter¶

  • The axis parameter allows to specify whether to fill by column (axis={0, rows}, default) or by row (axis={1, columns})
In [55]:
print(f"DataFrame df_nan:\n{df_nan}\n")
print(f"df_nan.interpolate(axis=1) interpolates NaN values by row: \n{df_nan.interpolate(axis=1)}\n")

DataFrame df_nan:
     A    B    C    D
0  4.0  3.0  3.0  1.0
1  1.0  NaN  NaN  2.0
2  3.0  2.0  1.0  NaN
3  NaN  NaN  NaN  NaN

df_nan.interpolate(axis=1) interpolates NaN values by row: 
     A         B         C    D
0  4.0  3.000000  3.000000  1.0
1  1.0  1.333333  1.666667  2.0
2  3.0  2.000000  1.000000  1.0
3  NaN       NaN       NaN  NaN

Duplicate Data in Pandas¶

  • Duplicate data is a common issue in data analysis
    • Consists of repeated or identical data
    • Notice that in duplicates both index and values are identical
  • Pandas includes methods to easily detect and handle duplicate data
    • duplicated returns a Boolean Series indicating which rows are duplicates
    • drop_duplicates returns a DataFrame with duplicate rows removed
      • drop_duplicates has a subset parameter to specify which columns to consider for duplicates

Identifying and Removing Duplicates¶

In [56]:
df_dup = pd.DataFrame({"col1": ["a", "b", "a", "a", "b"],  "col2": [1, 1, 2, 1, 1]})
print(f"DataFrame df_dup:\n{df_dup}\n")
print(f"df_dup.duplicated() returns a boolean Series with True for duplicated rows: \n{df_dup.duplicated()}\n")
print(f"df_dup.drop_duplicates() drops duplicated rows: \n{df_dup.drop_duplicates()}\n")

DataFrame df_dup:
  col1  col2
0    a     1
1    b     1
2    a     2
3    a     1
4    b     1

df_dup.duplicated() returns a boolean Series with True for duplicated rows: 
0    False
1    False
2    False
3     True
4     True
dtype: bool

df_dup.drop_duplicates() drops duplicated rows: 
  col1  col2
0    a     1
1    b     1
2    a     2

Duplicated Index Labels in Pandas¶

  • Using duplicate index labels it's generally not recommended as data selection becomes messy
    • Indexing a label with multiple entries returns a Series
    • Indexing a label with a single entry returns a scalar value
  • Usually happens because of a mis-specified multi-index
    • e.g., it shoud be obs-year but it is only obs
  • If you are getting unexpected results, check if your labels are unique
    • The is_unique property can be used to check if axis labels are unique
In [58]:
ser7 = pd.Series(np.arange(5), index=["a", "a", "b", "b", "c"])
print(f"Series with duplicate index labels: \n{ser7}\n")
print(f"ser7.index.is_unique checks for unique index labels and returns: {ser7.index.is_unique}\n")

Series with duplicate index labels: 
a    0
a    1
b    2
b    3
c    4
dtype: int64

ser7.index.is_unique checks for unique index labels and returns: False

Duplicated Index Labels in Pandas¶

In [59]:
# Data selection with duplicate labels
print(f"ser7['a'] returns a Series when the index label is duplicated: \n{ser7['a']}\n")
print(f"ser7['c'] returns a scalar when the index label is unique: {ser7['c']}\n")

ser7['a'] returns a Series when the index label is duplicated: 
a    0
a    1
dtype: int64

ser7['c'] returns a scalar when the index label is unique: 4

Data Loading and Writing¶

Data Loading and Writing¶

  • Data loading is a necessary initial step in (almost) any data analysis
  • The main categories of Input/Output (I/O) operations are:
    1. Reading/writing text files and (more efficient) formats stored on the computer
    2. Loading/updating data from databases
    3. Interfacing with network sources like APIs and web scraping
  • We will have a quick look at the first point
  • More resources on this topic: Ch.6 of Python for Data Analysis

Data Loading and Writing in Pandas¶

  • Pandas provides several methods to handle various data formats
    • CSV, Excel, JSON, HTML, SQL, etc.

Pandas Data Loading Functions¶

Function Description
read_csv Load delimited data from a file, URL, or file-like object; use comma as default delimiter
read_excel Read tabular data from an Excel XLS or XLSX file
read_fwf Read data in fixed-width column format (i.e., no delimiters)
read_pickle Read an object stored by pandas using the Python pickle format
read_parquet Read the Apache Parquet binary file format
read_json Read data from a JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) string representation, file, URL, or file-like object
read_sas Read a SAS dataset stored in one of the SAS system's custom storage formats
read_spss Read a data file created by SPSS
read_sql Read the results of a SQL query (using SQLAlchemy)
read_sql_table Read a whole SQL table (using SQLAlchemy); equivalent to using a query that selects everything in that table using read_sql
read_stata Read a dataset from Stata file format
read_xml Read a table of data from an XML file
read_feather Read the Feather binary file format
read_clipboard Variation of read_csv that reads data from the clipboard; useful for converting tables from web pages
read_hdf Read HDF5 files written by pandas
read_html Read all tables found in the given HTML document
read_orc Read the Apache ORC binary file format

Handling Complex Data Encoded as Text with Pandas¶

  • Pandas provides many optional arguments in data loading functions
    • Real-world data is often complex and these parameters allows to handle various scenarios
    • pandas.read_csv has around 50 optional parameters
      • Text-encoded data is very common and text has not been designed for data storage
  • The complexity of data loading function can be overwhelming
    • The pandas documentation on data loading functions provides extensive examples
    • If you face difficulties in reading a file, there is probably a relevant example that can provide insights

Optional Arguments in Data Loading Functions¶

  • Arguments for: Indexing and naming
    • Allows to set one or more columns as the DataFrame index
    • There are options to get the column names from the file, from provided arguments, or use a numeric index (default)

Optional Arguments in Data Loading Functions¶

  • Arguments for: Type Inference and Data Conversion
    • Purposefully designed data formats (e.g., pickle, excel) store data types, so loading is easy
      • For other formats (e.g., csv), the type of each column is not specified
      • In these cases pandas tries to guess the data type of each column
      • Usually it works but, if needed, pandas allows to specify the type by column
        • Allow to perform user-defined value conversions (flag-values)
        • Customization for handling missing value markers

Optional Arguments in Data Loading Functions¶

  • Date and Time Parsing
    • Features for combining date and time information
    • Ability to merge data spread across multiple columns into a single column
  • Iterating
    • Support for processing large files by dividing them into chunks
  • Handling Unclean Data
    • Options for skipping rows, footers, or comments
    • Capabilities to deal with minor data issues like numeric data with comma-separated thousands

Exploring Data Loading Functions Arguments with Examples¶

  • We will now explore some of the most common arguments in data loading functions

  • IT is a comma-separated-value CSV file with a header row and 3 rows of data

Loading a Text File with a Custom Separator - sep¶

  • Some text-format data file uses a given character as delimiter (e.g., csv use commas, tsv use tabs, etc.)
    • In these cases you can use the sep parameter to specify the delimiter (sep = \t)
  • Sep also accepts regular expressions to handle more complex cases
    • Regular expressions are a powerful tool for pattern matching
      • E.g., \s+ matches any whitespace character (space, tab, newline, etc.), ;|, matches a semicolon or a comma
    • Regular expressions are a very powerful tool, but also very complex
      • AI is very good to come up with them, but you need to know what/how to ask
      • You can start learning and test RegEx here: regex101

Loading a Text File with Variable Whitespace as Delimiters¶

  • Data in textual format may use variable whitespace

  • We can then use the regular expression \s+ to handle this case

Loading a Text File with Variable Whitespace as Delimiters¶

Handling Missing Values in File Reading¶

  • Missing data handling is crucial in file reading
  • Missing values typically appear as empty strings or sentinel values
  • Pandas has a set of sentinel values that are recognized as missing values by default:
    • E.g., NaN, NA, -1.#IND, 1.#QNAN, 1.#IND, -1.#QNAN, #N/A N/A, #N/A, N/A, n/a, NA, <NA>, #NA, NULL, null, NaN, -NaN, nan, -nan, ``
  • The na_values parameter allows to specify additional strings to be recognized as missing values
  • Specifying keep_default_na=False allows to not consider the default sentinel values

Loading a Text with Missing Values¶

  • Consider for example the following dataset
    • It has one NA value in the row 1 and an empty string in row 2

Useful Arguments for read.csv¶

Argument Description
path String indicating filesystem location, URL, or file-like object.
sep or delimiter Character sequence or regular expression to use to split fields in each row.
header Row number to use as column names; defaults to 0 (first row), but should be None if there is no header row.
index_col Column numbers or names to use as the row index in the result; can be a single name/number or a list of them for a hierarchical index.
names List of column names for result.
skiprows Number of rows at beginning of file to ignore or list of row numbers (starting from 0) to skip.
na_values Sequence of values to replace with NA. They are added to the default list unless keep_default_na=False is passed.
keep_default_na Whether to use the default NA value list or not (True by default).
comment Character(s) to split comments off the end of lines.
parse_dates Attempt to parse data to datetime; False by default. If True, will attempt to parse all columns. Otherwise, can specify a list of column numbers or names to parse. If element of list is tuple or list, will combine multiple columns together and parse to date.
keep_date_col If joining columns to parse date, keep the joined columns; False by default.
converters Dictionary containing column number or name mapping to functions (e.g., {"foo": f} would apply the function f to all values in the "foo" column).
dayfirst When parsing potentially ambiguous dates, treat as international format (e.g., 7/6/2012 -> June 7, 2012); False by default.
date_parser Function to use to parse dates.
nrows Number of rows to read from beginning of file (not counting the header).
iterator Return a TextFileReader object for reading the file piecemeal. This object can also be used with the with statement.
chunksize For iteration, size of file chunks.
skip_footer Number of lines to ignore at end of file.
verbose Print various parsing information, like the time spent in each stage of the file conversion and memory use information.
encoding Text encoding (e.g., "utf-8 for UTF-8 encoded text). Defaults to "utf-8" if None.
squeeze If the parsed data contains only one column, return a Series.
thousands Separator for thousands (e.g., "," or "."); default is None.
decimal Decimal separator in numbers (e.g., "." or ","); default is ".".
engine CSV parsing and conversion engine to use; can be one of "c", "python", or "pyarrow". The default is "c", though the newer "pyarrow" engine can parse some files much faster. The "python" engine is slower but supports some features that the other engines do not.

Writing Data to Text Files¶

  • Data can be exported to a text delimited format using to_csv
  • Main arguments:
    • The path_or_buf the filepath where to write the file
    • The sep parameter specifies the delimiter
      • The default is the comma
    • The index and header (True/False) set whether to write the index and header
      • The default is to write both
    • The na_rep parameter specifies the string to use in place of missing values
      • The default is to write them as empty strings
    • columns allows to specify the columns to be saved (and their order)
      • The default is to write all columns

Binary Data Formats - Pickle¶

  • Binary data formats are typically more efficient to read and write
    • They are designed to store data as it appears in the computer's memory
    • They are not human-readable
  • Storing data in binary format can be done using Python's pickle module
  • You can read a pickle file using read_pickle and write it using to_pickle

Iteration and Vectorization in Pandas¶

Iterating over Pandas DataFrames¶

  • Iterating over Pandas DataFrames is not recommended
    • Pandas is optimized for vectorized operations - iterating over rows is slow
    • Still, iteration is the most flexible tool, so sometimes it is necessary
  • You can iterate using any index method (bracket, loc, iloc)
    • The index method (df.index) returns a Series with the indexes for each row
    • You can use these indexes to select each row in a loop
  • Iterrows is a specificaly designed method for iterating over rows
    • It returns a tuple of two elements containing the index and row values

Iterating over Pandas DataFrames - Standard Indexing¶

In [77]:
df_iter = pd.DataFrame({'Student': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie', 'Ethan', 'Diana'], 'Score': [85, 58, 90, 45, 73]})
print(f"The df_iter dataFrame is: \n{df_iter}\n")
for index in df_iter.index: # Loop over the index of the dataFrame
    print(f"Student at index {index} is {df_iter['Student'].iloc[index]} and scored {df_iter['Score'].iloc[index]}")

The df_iter dataFrame is: 
   Student  Score
0    Alice     85
1      Bob     58
2  Charlie     90
3    Ethan     45
4    Diana     73

Student at index 0 is Alice and scored 85
Student at index 1 is Bob and scored 58
Student at index 2 is Charlie and scored 90
Student at index 3 is Ethan and scored 45
Student at index 4 is Diana and scored 73

Iterating over Pandas DataFrames - iterrows¶

In [78]:
print(f"The df_iter dataFrame is: \n{df_iter}\n")
for index, row in df_iter.iterrows():
    print(f"Student at index {index} is {row['Student']} and scored {row['Score']}")

The df_iter dataFrame is: 
   Student  Score
0    Alice     85
1      Bob     58
2  Charlie     90
3    Ethan     45
4    Diana     73

Student at index 0 is Alice and scored 85
Student at index 1 is Bob and scored 58
Student at index 2 is Charlie and scored 90
Student at index 3 is Ethan and scored 45
Student at index 4 is Diana and scored 73

DataFrame's Apply Method in Pandas¶

  • The apply method in Pandas is the 'intended' way to apply functions to a DataFrame
  • Not needed for array statistics commonly used(e.g., sum and mean)
    • df.sum() and df.mean() are equivalent to df.apply(sum) and df.apply(mean)
  • Most useful with user-defined functions

Advantages of Using Functions¶

  • A function is a "chunk" of code that takes inputs (parameters) and provides an output (return value)
  • In principle, it could be substituted by copy-pasting the code. However functions allow for:
    1. Evocative Naming: Can be assigned an evocative name, making the code easier to understand
    2. Centralized Code Updates: Only need to update code in one place when needed
    3. Reduced Error Risk: Eliminate the chance of incidental mistakes when copy-pasting
    4. Exploit Pandas's apply: Operate on the elements of multiple rows/columns without iteration
  • Best Practices:
    • Functions should do only one thing and do it well
    • Create a function if you find yourself copying and pasting the same code more than twice

Defining a Function in Python¶

def function_name(parameters, separated, by, commas):
    """docstring""" # to describe what the functions do - optional but advised
    body_doing_operations_on_parameters_and_storing_result
    return result
  • def: Keyword to start a function definition
  • function_name: Unique identifier for the function
  • parameters: Variables to pass to the function
  • docstring: Optional, for documentation of what the function does
  • body: Code block where the function's tasks are performed
  • return: Keyword to return a value from the function
    • if not specified the last line of the body is returned

An Example of Function Definition in Python¶

  • Function pass_or_fail:
    • input: score on the test
    • output: "Pass" if the score is above the passing_threshold and "Fail" otherwise
In [79]:
def pass_or_fail(score, passing_threshold):
    """Determines if the score is a pass or fail based on the passing threshold.""" #Docstring describing the function
    if score < 0 or score > 100:                                                    #Check if the score has an admissible value
        return "Invalid score"                                                      #Of the score value is not admissible return "Invalid score"
    if score >= passing_threshold:                                                  #Check if the the score is bigger or equal to the passing_threshold
        return "PASSED"                                                             #If the the score is bigger or equal to the passing_threshold return "Passed"
    else:                                                                           #Otherwise
        return "FAILED"                                                             #Return "FAILED"
print(f"pass_or_fail(score=85, passing_threshold=60) returns: {pass_or_fail(score=85, passing_threshold=60)}")
print(f"pass_or_fail(score=50, passing_threshold=60) returns: {pass_or_fail(score=50, passing_threshold=60)}")
print(f"pass_or_fail(score=110, passing_threshold=60) returns: {pass_or_fail(score=110, passing_threshold=60)}")

pass_or_fail(score=85, passing_threshold=60) returns: PASSED
pass_or_fail(score=50, passing_threshold=60) returns: FAILED
pass_or_fail(score=110, passing_threshold=60) returns: Invalid score

apply a Custom Function on a Series¶

Let's use the function pass_or_fail to create a new column identifying which students passed the test

In [80]:
print(f"The df_iter dataFrame is: \n{df_iter}\n")
print(f"Running df_iter['Result'] = df_iter['Score'].apply(pass_or_fail, passing_threshold=55), creates a new column with the result of the function on the Score column\n")
df_iter['Result'] = df_iter['Score'].apply(pass_or_fail, passing_threshold=55)
print(f"The exam_results becomes: \n{df_iter}\n")

The df_iter dataFrame is:

1      Bob     58

3    Ethan     45
4    Diana     73

Running df_iter['Result'] = df_iter['Score'].apply(pass_or_fail, passing_threshold=55), creates a new column with the result of the function on the Score column

The exam_results becomes:

1      Bob     58  PASSED
2  Charlie     90  PASSED
3    Ethan     45  FAILED
4    Diana     73  PASSED

map: a Limited but Faster apply¶

  • apply is flexible: can operate on multiple dataFrame columns and the function can take multiple arguments
  • map is a simpler method that:
    • Only operates on Series
    • Only accepts single-argument functions
    • Is typically more efficient
  • Use cases
    • Use map for single column transformations
    • Opt for apply in more elaborate cases

map a Limited but Faster apply¶

  • Let's define a simple function that extracts the last 3 characters of a string
In [81]:
def lastThreeChars(x):
    """Returns the last three characters of a string."""
    return x[-3:]
print(f"Running df2['state'].map(lastThreeChars) returns: \n{df2['state'].map(lastThreeChars)}\n")

Running df2['state'].map(lastThreeChars) returns: 
a    hio
b    hio
c    hio
d    ada
e    ada
f    ada
Name: state, dtype: object

apply a Custom Function on a DataFrame - Using Multiple Columns¶

  • apply allows to define functions that combine multiple columns
  • Let's define a function that returns the ratio of two columns
In [82]:
print(f"The function calculate_debt_to_income(row), calculates the ratio of the columns 'debt' and 'income'")
def calculate_debt_to_income(row):
    if row['income'] != 0:
        return row['debt'] / row['income']
    else:
        return np.nan

The function calculate_debt_to_income(row), calculates the ratio of the columns 'debt' and 'income'

apply a Custom Function on a DataFrame - Using Multiple Columns¶

In [83]:
print(f"df2 is:\n{df2}\n")
df2['debt_to_income'] = df2.apply(calculate_debt_to_income, axis=1)
print(f"df2['debt_to_income'] = df2.apply(calculate_debt_to_income, axis=1) creates a new column 'debt_to_income' in df2:\n{df2}")

Lambda Functions in Python: Simplifying Short Operations¶

  • Sometimes you only need to do an operation once
    • Defining a function in these cases is overkill
  • Lambda functions are anonymous functions that can be defined in a single line
    • Ideal for simple, temporary functions
  • Syntax:
    lambda parameters_separated_by_commas: body_doing_operations_on_parameters
  • Consists of the lambda keyword, followed by the parameters, a colon, and an expression
    • Can have any number of parameters but only one expression
    • The expression is evaluated and returned

Lambda Functions in Python: Simplifying Short Operations - An Example¶

In [84]:
print(f"Running df2['state'].apply(lambda x: x[-3:]) returns: \n{df2['state'].apply(lambda x: x[-3:])}\n")

Running df2['state'].apply(lambda x: x[-3:]) returns: 
a    hio
b    hio
c    hio
d    ada
e    ada
f    ada
Name: state, dtype: object

Group Operations in Pandas¶

Group Operations¶

  • Group operations:
    • Split a dataset into groups
    • Apply a function to each group independently
    • Combine the results into a data structure
  • Computing how a measure varies across groups:
    • Allow to characterize the measure (its distribution, its mean) for each group
      • E.g., how the height of children varies across schools
    • Allows to see how the measure varies across groups $\rightarrow$ investigate its relationship with the group variable
      • E.g., how the height of children varies with exposure to pollutants

Understanding the Split-Apply-Combine Strategy in pandas¶

  • A Three-Stage Process:
    1. Splitting:
      • Dividing the data (Pandas dataFrame) into groups based on one or more keys
    2. Applying:
      • Performing a function on each group
      • This will create a new object that might be:
        • Scalar (resulting from an aggregation, e.g., count, sum)
        • Composite (e.g., dataFrame or Series)
    3. Combining:
      • Aggregating the results from each group into a single result object
        • The structure of the result depends on the operation performed

Split-Apply-Combine - An Example Splitting by Key and Applying sum¶

Grouping Keys¶

  • Grouping keys can vary in type:
    1. Column Names: Of the DataFrame to be grouped (most common)
    2. List/Array: Directly specifying the groups (the length must match with the axis to group)
    3. Dictionary/Series: Groups together obs whose index is associated to the same value in the Dictionary/Series
    4. Index Levels: Groups together obs with the same value in a given level of a multiindex
    5. Function: Groups together obs with the same function(index) result

An Example Dataset to Group¶

In [85]:
dfGroup = pd.DataFrame({ "key1" : ["a", "a", "a", None, "b", "b", None], 
                    "key2" : pd.Series([1, 2, 1, 2, 1, None, 1], dtype="Int64"), 
                    "data1" : np.arange(0,7), 
                    "data2" : np.arange(10,17)})
print(f"dfGroup is: \n{dfGroup}\n")

dfGroup is: 
   key1  key2  data1  data2
0     a     1      0     10
1     a     2      1     11
2     a     1      2     12
3  None     2      3     13
4     b     1      4     14
5     b  <NA>      5     15
6  None     1      6     16

Grouping using groupby¶

  • The groupby is the method to group rows in a DataFrame
    • This creates a GroupBy object (think of it as a collection of DataFrames, one for each group)
    • One of the most frequent keys used is a column name
    • E.g., grouped_oneKey = dfToGroup.groupby("key1")
    • It's an intermediate step augmenting the data with the group info
  • We can then define an aggregation method on the grouped object
    • We might want to calculate group means
      • We can use the mean method on the DataFrameGroupBy object
    • grouped_oneKey.mean() computes the mean for each group based on the key variable

An Example Dataset to Group¶

In [86]:
dfToGroup = pd.DataFrame({ "key1" : ["a", "a", "a", None, "b", "b", None], 
                    "key2" : pd.Series([1, 2, 1, 2, 1, None, 1], dtype="Int64"), 
                    "data1" : np.arange(0,7), 
                    "data2" : np.arange(10,17)})
print(f"dfToGroup is: \n{dfToGroup}\n")

dfToGroup is: 
   key1  key2  data1  data2
0     a     1      0     10
1     a     2      1     11
2     a     1      2     12
3  None     2      3     13
4     b     1      4     14
5     b  <NA>      5     15
6  None     1      6     16

Grouping - Using a Column Name as Key¶

In [87]:
dfGrouped_oneKey = dfToGroup.groupby("key1")
print(f"The object dfGrouped_oneKey, defined as dfGroup.groupby('key1') is: {dfGrouped_oneKey}\n")
print(f"The command dfGrouped_oneKey.mean() returns: \n{dfGrouped_oneKey.mean()}\n")

The object dfGrouped_oneKey, defined as dfGroup.groupby('key1') is: <pandas.core.groupby.generic.DataFrameGroupBy object at 0x12eec6a90>

The command dfGrouped_oneKey.mean() returns: 
          key2  data1  data2
key1                        
a     1.333333    1.0   11.0
b          1.0    4.5   14.5

Iterating over Groups - Understanding the GroupBy object¶

  • The GroupBy object is a collection of DataFrames, one for each group
  • If you use it as an iterable it returns a tuple with:
    • The group key
    • The group DataFrame
  • Great for exploring the data and debugging (and understanding the groupby operation)

Iterating over Groups - Understanding the GroupBy object¶

In [88]:
for name, group in dfGrouped_oneKey:
    print(f"Group name: {name}")
    print(f"Group dataFrame:\n{group}\n")

Group name: a
Group dataFrame:
  key1  key2  data1  data2
0    a     1      0     10
1    a     2      1     11
2    a     1      2     12

Group name: b
Group dataFrame:
  key1  key2  data1  data2
4    b     1      4     14
5    b  <NA>      5     15
  • The dataFrame has been split into two groups based on the values of the key variable
  • Each column of each group is aggregated using the mean method
  • The result is a dataFrame with the mean of each column for each group

Grouping - Using Multiple Column Names as Key¶

In [89]:
dfGrouped_twoKeys = dfToGroup.groupby(['key1', 'key2'])
print(f"The object dfGrouped_twoKeys, defined as dfToGroup.groupby(['key1', 'key2']) is: {dfGrouped_twoKeys}\n")
print(f"The command dfGrouped_twoKeys.mean() returns: \n{dfGrouped_twoKeys.mean()}\n")

The object dfGrouped_twoKeys, defined as dfToGroup.groupby(['key1', 'key2']) is: <pandas.core.groupby.generic.DataFrameGroupBy object at 0x12eed8590>

The command dfGrouped_twoKeys.mean() returns: 
           data1  data2
key1 key2              
a    1       1.0   11.0
     2       1.0   11.0
b    1       4.0   14.0
  • Grouping by two or more keys creates groups based on all the combinations of their values
    • Hierarchical indexing

Grouping - Using arrays/Lists as Key¶

In [90]:
key_states = np.array(["OH", "CA", "CA", "OH", "OH", "CA", "OH"])
key_years = [2005, 2005, 2006, 2005, 2006, 2005, 2006]
print(f"The array 'key_states' and the List 'years' are:\n{key_states}\n{key_years}\n")
dfGrouped_twoKeys_al = dfToGroup.groupby([key_states, key_years])
print(f"These objects can be used as keys on dfToGroup using grouped_twoKeys_al = dfToGroup.groupby([key_states, key_years])\n")
print(f"The command grouped_twoKeys_al.mean(numeric_only=True) returns:\n{dfGrouped_twoKeys_al.mean(numeric_only=True)}\n")

The array 'key_states' and the List 'years' are:
['OH' 'CA' 'CA' 'OH' 'OH' 'CA' 'OH']
[2005, 2005, 2006, 2005, 2006, 2005, 2006]

These objects can be used as keys on dfToGroup using grouped_twoKeys_al = dfToGroup.groupby([key_states, key_years])

The command grouped_twoKeys_al.mean(numeric_only=True) returns:
         key2  data1  data2
CA 2005   2.0    3.0   13.0
   2006   1.0    2.0   12.0
OH 2005   1.5    1.5   11.5
   2006   1.0    5.0   15.0
  • Notice that we added the option numeric_only=True to avoid errors for computing the mean of the non-numeric column 'key1'

Grouping - Using Series/Dictionaries as Key¶

  • Using a Series/Dictionary as key maps the index of the DataFrame to the associated value
In [91]:

In [92]:
dfGrouped_oneKey_s = dfToGroup.groupby(key_plants)

  • Gouping can be done based on the levels of a MultiIndex
    • This is done by specifying the level number or name
    • E.g., df.groupby(level="level_name")

Grouping - Apply the Function length on the Index to Define the Key¶

Let's say that we want to group the data by the length of index names of the following dataset

Grouping - Apply a Lambda Function on a Column to Define the Key¶

  • In some cases it is useful to group on a function of the value of a column
  • Let's consider the familiar df2 DataFrame
    • We will group observations by brackets of popoulation size
In [98]:
print(f"df2 is:\n{df2}")

df2 is:
   year   state      pop          debt  income  debt_to_income
a  2000    Ohio  1500000  1.200000e+09     NaN             NaN

c  2002    Ohio  3600000  1.700000e+09     NaN             NaN
d  2001  Nevada  2400000  5.000000e+08  3000.0   166666.666667
e  2002  Nevada  2900000  8.000000e+08     NaN             NaN
f  2003  Nevada  3200000  1.000000e+09  4000.0   250000.000000

Grouping - Apply a Lambda Function on a Column to Define the Key¶

  • We define a lambda function that:
    • If the population is greater than 200 thousands, returns "Big Pop"
    • Otherwise, returns "Small Pop"
  • Applying this function to the population column returns a series
    • Whose index matches the DataFrame one
    • Whose values are either 'Big Pop' or 'Small Pop'

Grouping - Apply a Lambda Function on a Column to Define the Key¶

In [99]:
print(f"""The command
df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop')
returns the series:\n{df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop')}""")

The command
df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop')
returns the series:
a    Small Pop
b    Small Pop
c      Big Pop
d      Big Pop
e      Big Pop
f      Big Pop
Name: pop, dtype: object

Grouping - Using Functions to Define Key¶

  • Python functions offer the most flexible method for defining group
  • These functions are executed on each index value by default
    • Can also be applied to the values of a column
  • The function's return values determine the group names

Grouping - Use the Output of a Lambda Function to Group and Aggregate¶

  • We can then use the series to group the dataset
  • Finally we run the aggregating function sum on the grouped object
In [100]:
print(f"""We can use this series to compute an aggregate function on the columns 'debt' and 'income' by running:
df2[['debt', 'income']].groupby(df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop')).sum():\n{df2[['debt', 'income']].groupby(df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop')).sum()}""") 

We can use this series to compute an aggregate function on the columns 'debt' and 'income' by running:
df2[['debt', 'income']].groupby(df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop')).sum():
                   debt  income
pop                            
Big Pop    4.000000e+09  7000.0
Small Pop  2.700000e+09  2000.0
  1. The command df2['pop'].apply(lambda x: 'Big Pop' if x > 2000000 else 'Small Pop') returns a series
    • The index is the same as the DataFrame, the values is 'Big Pop'/'Small Pop' depending on 'pop'
  2. The series is used to group the subset DataFrame (['debt', 'income'] )
  3. sum the values of observations belonging to the grouped subset DataFrame

Data Aggregation in Pandas¶

  • Aggregations are transformations yielding scalar values
    • They reduce the dimensionality of the data
    • Common aggregations include mean, count, min, sum
    • Pandas optimizes these operations for efficiency
  • Aggregations can be applied to a GroupBy object
    • Not limited to predefined methods/functions
      • Custom aggregation functions can be applied
      • Use .aggregate() or .agg() with custom functions

Some Aggregation Functions in Pandas¶

Function name Description
any, all Return True if any (one or more values) or all non-NA values are True
count Number of non-NA values
first, last First and last non-NA values
mean Mean of non-NA values
median Arithmetic median of non-NA values
min, max Minimum and maximum of non-NA values
nth Retrieve value that would appear at position n with the data in sorted order
ohlc Compute four "open-high-low-close" statistics for time series-like data
prod Product of non-NA values
quantile Compute sample quantile
rank Ordinal ranks of non-NA values, like calling Series.rank
size Compute group sizes, returning result as a Series
sum Sum of non-NA values
std, var Sample standard deviation and variance

Data Aggregation in Pandas - Some Examples¶

In [101]:

print(f"dfGrouped_oneKey.first() returns the first element of each sorted group: \n{dfGrouped_oneKey.first()}\n")

Data Aggregation in Pandas - Using Custom Functions¶

    return x.max() - x.min()

Using Multiple/Different Functions on Different Columns¶

  • Multiple functions can be applied at once to different columns
    • Use a list specifying the functions
  • If the functions that you want to apply are different for each column
    • Use a dictionary with the column names as keys and the functions to apply as values

Using Multiple/Different Functions on Different Columns¶

In [103]:
print(f"dfGrouped_oneKey.agg(['mean', 'median']) returns: \n{dfGrouped_oneKey.agg(['mean', 'median'])}\n")
dict_col_fun = {"data1" : ["mean", "median"], "data2" : range_func}
print(f"The column:functions dictionary dict_col_fun is: \n{dict_col_fun}\n")
print(f"dfGrouped_oneKey.agg(dict_col_fun) returns: \n{dfGrouped_oneKey.agg(dict_col_fun)}\n")

dfGrouped_oneKey.agg(['mean', 'median']) returns: 
          key2        data1        data2       
          mean median  mean median  mean median
key1

b          1.0    1.0   4.5    4.5  14.5   14.5

The column:functions dictionary dict_col_fun is: 
{'data1': ['mean', 'median'], 'data2': <function range_func at 0x12ee7dd00>}

dfGrouped_oneKey.agg(dict_col_fun) returns: 
     data1             data2
      mean median range_func
key1                        
a      1.0    1.0          2
b      4.5    4.5          1

Data Aggregation in Pandas - apply Always The Most Flexible Option¶

  • As we saw, map is a faster but limited version of apply on non-grouped data
    • The aggregate method is the fast but limited apply for grouped data
      • It is intended for scalar output
  • The apply method is always the most flexible option
    • It can take any function returning a Pandas object (DataFrame or Series) or a scalar
    • Applies to all the groups
    • It will then attempt to combine the pieces
  • Use apply when:
    • The output of the transformation is a DataFrame or Series
    • The transformation needs the data from multiple columns
    • The transformation needs additional parameters (other than the column data)

Data Aggregation Using apply - An Example¶

  • We will now see a example of using apply to perform a group operation in a slightly less "toy" setting
  • We will use the dataset "tips" (it comes with the seaborn library but we use a modified version)
    • Our aim is to uncover some features of the distribution of tips
    • We want to identify the highest n top and bottom tips in percentage by groups based on day/time combination

Data Aggregation Using apply - The Steps of the Example¶

  1. Data Import
  2. Definition of a function compute_pctTip_topBot
    1. Computes the tip percentage of a bill
    2. Select the highest n top and bottom tips in percentage
  3. Application of the function by groups based on day/time combination
  4. Refinements to improve readability (CRUCIAL!) of the table result
  5. Saving the result to a file
