Some Info on the tips Dataset¶

The dataset tips contains information about tips in a restaurant:

  • total_bill: Total bill (cost of the meal), including tax, in US dollars
  • tip: Tip amount in US dollars
  • sex: Gender of the person attending the table
  • smoker: Indicates whether the table was in the smoking area or not
  • day: Day of the week
  • time: Meal (e.g., Lunch, Dinner)
  • size: Number of people in the party

Grouping by day/time Combination¶

  • The dataset provides the keys that we need for grouping in the columns day and time
  • We need to define the function to apply to each group and extract the information that we need

Function Definition - compute_pctTip_topBot¶

In [105]:
# Defining the function compute_ratio_topBottom
def compute_pctTip_topBot(group, n):
    # Calculate the percentage of tip from the total bill and add it as a new column 'pctTip'
    group['pctTip'] = 100 * group['tip'] / group['total_bill']
    # Select the top n rows with the highest 'pctTip' values
    top_n = group.nlargest(n, 'pctTip')
    # Select the bottom n rows with the lowest 'pctTip' values
    bottom_n = group.nsmallest(n, 'pctTip')
    # Concatenate the top and bottom rows into a single DataFrame
    #more on this soon, concatenate stacks the two dataframes one on top of the other
    result = pd.concat([top_n, bottom_n]) 
    # Return the combined DataFrame
    return result

Apply the Function compute_pctTip_topBot by day/time Groups¶

In [106]:
# Grouping the 'tips' DataFrame by 'day' and 'time', and applying the function to each group
tips.groupby(['day', 'time']).apply(compute_pctTip_topBot, n=2)

# Map the weekday names to their corresponding numerical values
weekday_map = {'Mon': 1, 'Tue': 2, 'Wed': 3, 'Thur': 4, 'Fri': 5, 'Sat': 6, 'Sun': 7}
# Map the meal times (e.g., 'Lunch', 'Dinner') to numerical values for sorting
time_map = {'Lunch': 1, 'Dinner': 2}
# Apply the weekday mapping to the 'day' column, creating a new column 'day_order'
tips['day_order'] = tips['day'].map(weekday_map)
# Apply the time mapping to the 'time' column, creating a new column 'time_order'
tips['time_order'] = tips['time'].map(time_map)

Saving the Table with Results to a File¶

  • Now that we have the table with the results, we can save it to a file
    1. We will save it into markdown using the to_markdown method
      • The format used in jupyter notebooks
    2. We will save it to excel using the to_excel method,
      • A common format in the corporate world
  • Both methods have several options to customize the output
    • Check the help for more details (e.g., df_pctTip_topBot_by_dayTime.to_excel?)
In [111]:
# Save the DataFrame to a Markdown file with GitHub-flavored markdown (requires to install the 'tabulate package')
df_pctTip_topBot_by_dayTime.to_markdown(os.path.join('tables', 'df_pctTip_topBot_by_dayTime.md'), tablefmt="github")
# Save the DataFrame to an Excel file with better formatting
df_pctTip_topBot_by_dayTime.to_excel(os.path.join('tables', 'df_pctTip_topBot_by_dayTime.xlsx'), sheet_name='Top_bottom_tips_time_meal')

The Saved Table in Excel¶

Working with Multiple Data Objects in Pandas¶

Index Alignment for Arithmetic Operations¶

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment¶

  • Pandas simplifies doing operations on multiple objects by accounting for their indexes
  • When performing arithmetic operations and other data transformations, Pandas automatically aligns indexes
    • The resulting index is the union of the indexes of the two Pandas objects
    • If index pairs don't match, missing values (NaN) are introduced

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in Series¶

In [112]:
ser3 = pd.Series([7.3, -2.9, 3.4], index=["a", "c", "d"])
ser4 = pd.Series([-2.1, 2.7, -1.5], index=["c", "a", "e",])
print(f"ser3 Series: \n{ser3}\n")
print(f"ser4 Series: \n{ser4}\n")
print(f"Result of ser3 + ser4: \n{ser3 + ser4}")

ser3 Series: 
a    7.3
c   -2.9
d    3.4
dtype: float64

ser4 Series: 
c   -2.1
a    2.7
e   -1.5
dtype: float64

Result of ser3 + ser4: 
a    10.0
c    -5.0
d     NaN
e     NaN
dtype: float64

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in Series¶

  • ser3 + ser4 yields a series with indexes a, c, d, e
    • Overlapping indexes (a and c) are matched in the operation
    • Non-overlapping indexes (d and e) return NaN

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in DataFrames¶

  • The default behavior of Pandas is to align series indexes with the dataFrame columns
    • The resulting index is the union of the indexes of the two Pandas objects
    • If index pairs don't match, missing values (NaN) are introduced (a union of the indexes)

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in DataFrames¶

In [113]:
df4 = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(9.).reshape((3, 3)).transpose(), columns=["Colorado", "Texas", "Ohio"], index=["Colorado", "Texas", "Ohio"])
print(f"DataFrame df4:\n{df4}\n")
ser5 = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["Colorado", "Texas", "Florida"])
print(f"Series ser5:\n{ser5}\n")
print(f"df4 + ser5 aligns the Series index with the DataFrame columns, broadcasting down the rows: \n{df4 + ser5}\n")

DataFrame df4:
          Colorado  Texas  Ohio
Colorado       0.0    3.0   6.0
Texas          1.0    4.0   7.0
Ohio           2.0    5.0   8.0

Series ser5:
Colorado    10
Texas       20
Florida     30
dtype: int64

df4 + ser5 aligns the Series index with the DataFrame columns, broadcasting down the rows: 
          Colorado  Florida  Ohio  Texas
Colorado      10.0      NaN   NaN   23.0
Texas         11.0      NaN   NaN   24.0
Ohio          12.0      NaN   NaN   25.0

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in DataFrames¶

  • With Pandas arithmentic methods (e.g., add), use axis=0 to align with the rows
In [114]:
print(f"DataFrame df4:\n{df4}\n")
print(f"Series ser5:\n{ser5}\n")
print(f"df4.add(ser5, axis=0) aligns the Series index with the DataFrame rows, broadcasting across the columns: \n{df4.add(ser5, axis=0)}\n")

DataFrame df4:
          Colorado  Texas  Ohio
Colorado       0.0    3.0   6.0
Texas          1.0    4.0   7.0
Ohio           2.0    5.0   8.0

Series ser5:
Colorado    10
Texas       20
Florida     30
dtype: int64

df4.add(ser5, axis=0) aligns the Series index with the DataFrame rows, broadcasting across the columns: 
          Colorado  Texas  Ohio
Colorado      10.0   13.0  16.0
Florida        NaN    NaN   NaN
Ohio           NaN    NaN   NaN
Texas         21.0   24.0  27.0

Panda's Arithmetic Methods¶

Method Description
add Method for addition
sub Method for subtraction
div Method for division
floordiv Method for floor division
mul Method for multiplication
mod Method for modulo operation
pow Method for exponential power

💼 Exercises: Using Index Alignment in Arithmetic Methods¶

Exercise 1: Exchange Rate Conversion¶

You have a DataFrame containing sales data for a multinational company in different countries. There is a column called "Sales Amount (USD)" that represents the sales amount in U.S. dollars. You also have an exchange rate Series that provides the exchange rates for converting the sales amount to the local currency of each country. Create a new column called "Sales Amount (Local Currency)" that converts the sales amount from USD to the local currency using the provided exchange rates.

# Sample sales data DataFrame
sales_data = {'Country': ['USA', 'Germany', 'Japan', 'China', 'India'],
              'Sales Amount (USD)': [5000, 3500, 6000, 8000, 4500]}

sales_df = pd.DataFrame(sales_data)

# Sample exchange rate Series
exchange_rates = pd.Series(data=[1.0, 0.85, 110.0, 6.35, 75.0],
                           index=['USA', 'Germany', 'Japan', 'China', 'India'],
                           name='Exchange Rate')

# Create a new column "Sales Amount (Local Currency)" in sales_df by converting USD to local currency

Exercise 2: GDP Growth Rate Calculation¶

Calculate the annual GDP growth rate for a list of countries. You are provided with two DataFrames: gdp_last_year and gdp_this_year, each containing the GDP values for various countries in the respective years. Add a new column to gdp_this_year DataFrame named "GDP Growth Rate (%)" that calculates the percentage growth rate from the previous year.

# GDP data for the last year
gdp_last_year = pd.DataFrame({'Country': ['USA', 'China', 'India', 'Germany', 'Brazil'],
                              'GDP': [21.43, 14.34, 2.87, 3.86, 1.84]})  # Trillions USD

# GDP data for this year
gdp_this_year = pd.DataFrame({'Country': ['USA', 'China', 'India', 'Germany', 'Brazil'],
                              'GDP': [22.32, 15.42, 3.05, 3.95, 1.92]})  # Trillions USD

# Calculate GDP Growth Rate and add as a new column to gdp_this_year DataFrame

Exercise 3: Portfolio Value Recalculation¶

Given a DataFrame portfolio containing the number of shares held in different companies and a Series stock_prices representing the current stock prices, calculate the total value of the portfolio for each company and add a new column "Total Value" to the portfolio DataFrame.

# Sample portfolio data
portfolio = pd.DataFrame({'Company': ['Apple', 'Google', 'Amazon', 'Tesla'],
                          'Shares': [50, 30, 20, 10]})

# Current stock prices
stock_prices = pd.Series(data=[150, 2800, 3300, 700],
                         index=['Apple', 'Google', 'Amazon', 'Tesla'],
                         name='Stock Price')

# Calculate Total Value of shares for each company and add as a new column to portfolio DataFrame

Exercise 4: Inflation Adjustment¶

Adjust the prices of a list of products over the years for inflation. You are given a DataFrame product_prices with columns "Year", "Product", and "Price". You also have a Series inflation_rate that provides the annual inflation rate. Create a new column "Adjusted Price" that adjusts the prices for inflation to the current year.

# Sample product prices data
product_prices = pd.DataFrame({'Year': [2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022],
                               'Product': ['Laptop', 'Laptop', 'Laptop', 'Laptop', 'Laptop'],

Working with Multiple Data Objects in Pandas¶

Data Concatenation and Merging¶

DataFrame Concatenation¶

  • Concatenating: Stacks datasets by axis
    • concat():
      • Stacks rows or binds columns (but for the columns merge is more flexible)
      • It is the method used when combining the result of groupby operations
      • Mostly used to stack rows using axis=0 and ignoring indexes using ignore_index=True

DataFrame Concatenation in Pandas - concat()- ignore_index=True¶

In [115]:
df9 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [ 3, 4]})
df10 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [5, 6], 'B': [7, 8]})
print(f"df9 is:\n{df9}\n\ndf10 is:\n{df10}\n")
print(f"The command pd.concat([df9, df10], axis=0, ignore_index=True) concatenates df9 and df10 along the rows: \n{pd.concat([df9, df10], axis=0, ignore_index=True)}\n")

df9 is:
   A  B
0  1  3
1  2  4

df10 is:
   A  B
0  5  7
1  6  8

The command pd.concat([df9, df10], axis=0, ignore_index=True) concatenates df9 and df10 along the rows: 
   A  B
0  1  3
1  2  4
2  5  7
3  6  8

DataFrame Concatenation in Pandas - concat()¶

In [116]:
print(f"df9 is:\n{df9}\n\ndf10 is:\n{df10}\n")
print(f"The command pd.concat([df9, df10], axis=0) concatenates df9 and df10 along the rows keeping the index: \n{pd.concat([df9, df10], axis=0)}\n")

df9 is:
   A  B
0  1  3
1  2  4

df10 is:
   A  B
0  5  7
1  6  8

The command pd.concat([df9, df10], axis=0) concatenates df9 and df10 along the rows keeping the index: 
   A  B
0  1  3
1  2  4
0  5  7
1  6  8

DataFrame Concatenation in Pandas - concat() - Different Index Names Along Concatenation¶

In [117]:
df11 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [11, 12], 'B': [13, 14]})
df12 = pd.DataFrame({'C': [15, 16], 'D': [17, 18]})
print(f"df11 is:\n{df11}\n\ndf12 is:\n{df12}\n")
print(f"""The command 
pd.concat([df11, df12], axis=0, ignore_index=True) concatenates df11 and df12 (with different column names) along the rows:
{pd.concat([df11, df12], axis=0, ignore_index=True)}\n""")

df11 is:
    A   B
0  11  13
1  12  14

df12 is:
    C   D
0  15  17
1  16  18

The command 
pd.concat([df11, df12], axis=0, ignore_index=True) concatenates df11 and df12 (with different column names) along the rows:
      A     B     C     D
0  11.0  13.0   NaN   NaN
1  12.0  14.0   NaN   NaN
2   NaN   NaN  15.0  17.0
3   NaN   NaN  16.0  18.0

Merging¶

  • Merging: Integrates dataframes columns based on ID/key
    • merge()is the most flexible function to merge

Syntax

pd.merge(df_a, df_b, on='key')
  • key sets the column(s) storing the information identifying the same observations across dataframes

The Different Kinds of Merge¶

  • Different kinds of merges can be performed using the parameter how
Option Behavior
how="inner" The output Dataframe keys are the intersection of the keys of both tables
how="left" The output Dataframe keys are the ones from the left table
how="right" The output Dataframe keys are the ones from the right table
how="outer" The output Dataframe keys are the union of the key from both tables

The Left Merge¶

  • We will focus on the left merge that is (allegedly) the most useful in data analysis
    • There is a main dataset (receiver) to augment with info from other datasets (donors)
    • E.g., An education economist investigating the impact of a policy on students' grades works with:
      • The core (receiver) dataset storing info on students' scores
      • Many other (donor) datasets providing info on timing of the policy and covariates
        • Socio-economic status, Age, Extracullicular activities, etc.

Doing a Left Merge in Pandas¶

  • The command pd.merge(df_a, df_b, on='key', how='left') does a left merge of df9 and df10 on their 'key' columns:
    • Observations in df_a (receiver) with matching 'key' in df_b (donor)
      • Receive the information of the columns of df_b
    • Observations in df_a (receiver) without matching 'key' in df_b (donor)
      • Are filled with NaN in the columns of df_b
    • Observations in df_b (donor) without matching 'key' in df_a (receiver)
      • Are dropped

DataFrame Merging - merge()¶

In [118]:
df_WA = pd.DataFrame({'ID': ['jin', 'luca', 'mazhar', 'lynne', 'massimo', 'matthew'],
                        'weight': [60, 70, 66, 50, 65, 60],
                        'age': [11, 12, 12, 13, 12, 12]}) 
df_HA = pd.DataFrame({ 'ID': ['luca', 'lynne', 'matthew', 'jin', 'massimo', 'mazhar'],
                        'height': [170, 178, 164, np.NAN, 180, 175],
                        'age': [12, 13, 12, 11, 12, 12,]}) 
print(f"data_WA is: \n{df_WA}\n")
print(f"data_HA is: \n{df_HA}\n")

data_WA is: 
        ID  weight  age
0      jin      60   11
1     luca      70   12
2   mazhar      66   12
3    lynne      50   13
4  massimo      65   12
5  matthew      60   12

data_HA is: 
        ID  height  age
0     luca   170.0   12
1    lynne   178.0   13
2  matthew   164.0   12
3      jin     NaN   11
4  massimo   180.0   12
5   mazhar   175.0   12

DataFrame Merging - merge()¶

In [119]:
print(f"pd.merge(df_WA, df_HA, on='ID', how='left') merges df_HA and df_WA on the 'ID' column using a left join: \n{pd.merge(df_WA, df_HA, on='ID', how='left')}\n")

pd.merge(df_WA, df_HA, on='ID', how='left') merges df_HA and df_WA on the 'ID' column using a left join: 
        ID  weight  age_x  height  age_y
0      jin      60     11     NaN     11
1     luca      70     12   170.0     12
2   mazhar      66     12   175.0     12
3    lynne      50     13   178.0     13
4  massimo      65     12   180.0     12
5  matthew      60     12   164.0     12

Join - A Simplified Index-Based Merge¶

  • join() is a simplified left-merging based on index labels
    • df_WA.join(df_HA) left-joins df_WA (receiver) and df_HA (donor) on their indexes
    • The parameters lsuffix and rsuffix add the suffixes to overlapping column names
      • The default suffixes are _x and _y
  • In this case the index do not represent the ID
    • This merge is CORRUPTING THE INFORMATION IN THE DATA
    • Any analysis based on this merge will be WRONG
    • We are just doing it for illustration purposes

Understanding DataFrame Merging in Pandas - join()¶

In [120]:
print(f"df_WA.join(df_HA, how='left') joins df_WA and df_HA on the index using a left join: \n{df_WA.join(df_HA, how='left', lsuffix='_dfWA', rsuffix='_dfHA')}\n")
print(f"df_WA.join(df_WA[['data2']], how='left') only adds the column of interest from df_WA: \n{df_WA.join(df_HA[['height']], how='left')}\n")

df_WA.join(df_HA, how='left') joins df_WA and df_HA on the index using a left join: 
   ID_dfWA  weight  age_dfWA  ID_dfHA  height  age_dfHA
0      jin      60        11     luca   170.0        12
1     luca      70        12    lynne   178.0        13
2   mazhar      66        12  matthew   164.0        12
3    lynne      50        13      jin     NaN        11
4  massimo      65        12  massimo   180.0        12
5  matthew      60        12   mazhar   175.0        12

df_WA.join(df_WA[['data2']], how='left') only adds the column of interest from df_WA: 
        ID  weight  age  height
0      jin      60   11   170.0
1     luca      70   12   178.0
2   mazhar      66   12   164.0
3    lynne      50   13     NaN
4  massimo      65   12   180.0
5  matthew      60   12   175.0

Strategy for Effective Merging - Check the Calls to Merge¶

Key Considerations for Merging DataFrames:

  • Potential for Errors:
    • Merging is a delicate process that might lead to data corruption
      • Countless cases of scientific and business analysis invalidated by merging errors
    • A careful and methodical approach is crucial to ensure data integrity
  • Always triple check when merging
    • You have just saw what might happen, and no warning nor error is raised
    • If the AI is doing merges, check them thoroughly

Strategy for Effective Merging - Common Problems¶

  • Often the results of a merge are not what you expect
    • Duplicates keys in one or both dataframes might lead to unexpected results
      • Multiple matches for the same key
    • Subtle differences in keys/ID can lead loss of information
      • Need to be of the same type (9 and "9" are different)
      • There might be small typing differences (e.g., "9" and " 9", "Padova" and "padova", "Nicolò" and "Nicolo'")
      • In these cases the merge will return more NaN that it should

Data Reshaping¶

Different Shapes of Data - Wide and Long¶

Different Shapes of Data - Use Cases¶

  • The shape of a given dataset depends on the preferences of the data provider
    • You might find data referring to the same observations in different shapes
    • It is then important to be able to reshape the data to merge them
  • Apart from data ingestion, different shapes are more convenient in different tasks
    • Depending on the function you want to perform, you need one shape or the other
  • Pandas provides methods to reshape data
    • stack() and unstack() are the most common ones
    • pivot() and melt() are more advanced and flexible

Reshaping in Pandas - Some Resources¶

  • Pandas provides a variety of methods to reshape data
    • stack() and unstack() are the most common ones
    • pivot() and melt() are more advanced and flexible

Working with Multiple Data Objects in Pandas¶

Index Alignment for Arithmetic Operations¶

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment¶

  • Pandas simplifies doing operations on multiple objects by accounting for their indexes
  • When performing arithmetic operations and other data transformations, Pandas automatically aligns indexes
    • The resulting index is the union of the indexes of the two Pandas objects
    • If index pairs don't match, missing values (NaN) are introduced

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in Series¶

In [121]:
ser3 = pd.Series([7.3, -2.9, 3.4], index=["a", "c", "d"])
ser4 = pd.Series([-2.1, 2.7, -1.5], index=["c", "a", "e",])
print(f"ser3 Series: \n{ser3}\n")
print(f"ser4 Series: \n{ser4}\n")
print(f"Result of ser3 + ser4: \n{ser3 + ser4}")

ser3 Series: 
a    7.3
c   -2.9
d    3.4
dtype: float64

ser4 Series: 
c   -2.1
a    2.7
e   -1.5
dtype: float64

Result of ser3 + ser4: 
a    10.0
c    -5.0
d     NaN
e     NaN
dtype: float64

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in Series¶

  • ser3 + ser4 yields a series with indexes a, c, d, e
    • Overlapping indexes (a and c) are matched in the operation
    • Non-overlapping indexes (d and e) return NaN

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in DataFrames¶

  • The default behavior of Pandas is to align series indexes with the dataFrame columns
    • The resulting index is the union of the indexes of the two Pandas objects
    • If index pairs don't match, missing values (NaN) are introduced (a union of the indexes)

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in DataFrames¶

In [122]:
df4 = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(9.).reshape((3, 3)).transpose(), columns=["Colorado", "Texas", "Ohio"], index=["Colorado", "Texas", "Ohio"])
print(f"DataFrame df4:\n{df4}\n")
ser5 = pd.Series([10, 20, 30], index=["Colorado", "Texas", "Florida"])
print(f"Series ser5:\n{ser5}\n")
print(f"df4 + ser5 aligns the Series index with the DataFrame columns, broadcasting down the rows: \n{df4 + ser5}\n")

DataFrame df4:
          Colorado  Texas  Ohio
Colorado       0.0    3.0   6.0
Texas          1.0    4.0   7.0
Ohio           2.0    5.0   8.0

Series ser5:
Colorado    10
Texas       20
Florida     30
dtype: int64

df4 + ser5 aligns the Series index with the DataFrame columns, broadcasting down the rows: 
          Colorado  Florida  Ohio  Texas
Colorado      10.0      NaN   NaN   23.0
Texas         11.0      NaN   NaN   24.0
Ohio          12.0      NaN   NaN   25.0

Arithmetic with Pandas - Automatic Index Alignment in DataFrames¶

  • With Pandas arithmentic methods (e.g., add), use axis=0 to align with the rows
In [123]:
print(f"DataFrame df4:\n{df4}\n")
print(f"Series ser5:\n{ser5}\n")
print(f"df4.add(ser5, axis=0) aligns the Series index with the DataFrame rows, broadcasting across the columns: \n{df4.add(ser5, axis=0)}\n")

DataFrame df4:
          Colorado  Texas  Ohio
Colorado       0.0    3.0   6.0
Texas          1.0    4.0   7.0
Ohio           2.0    5.0   8.0

Series ser5:
Colorado    10
Texas       20
Florida     30
dtype: int64

df4.add(ser5, axis=0) aligns the Series index with the DataFrame rows, broadcasting across the columns: 
          Colorado  Texas  Ohio
Colorado      10.0   13.0  16.0
Florida        NaN    NaN   NaN
Ohio           NaN    NaN   NaN
Texas         21.0   24.0  27.0

Panda's Arithmetic Methods¶

Method Description
add Method for addition
sub Method for subtraction
div Method for division
floordiv Method for floor division
mul Method for multiplication
mod Method for modulo operation
pow Method for exponential power

Merging¶

Strategy for Effective Merging - The Checks to Do When Merging¶

  • Check the keys/ID of each dataset for duplicates
  • Identify Non-Matching keys/ID Before Merging:
    • Identify the keys in the receiver dataframe that do not have a match in the donor dataframe
    • For these obs the donated columns will be NaN in the merged dataframe
    • Better to use indexes for this check
      • Allows to use the .index.get_level_values method
      • For multiindex DataFrames creates automatically the combinations of indexes

Strategy for Effective Merging - The Checks to Do When Merging¶

  • Prefer Adding Columns Individually:
    • Enhances code readability and manageability
    • Adding one column at a time makes it easier track NaN values and perform the checks below:
      1. Check the NaN in the column to be received
        • The column stored in the donor dataframe
        • If there are NaN values they will pass to the receiver dataframe
      2. Check the NaN in the column received
        • The column stored in the receiver dataframe (only available after the merge)
        • The number of NaN should be equal to the sum of:
          • The number of NaN in the donor dataframe plus
          • the number of indexes/keys/ID in the receiver not in the donor

Strategy for Effective Merging - The Datasets¶

  • Let's create two datasets to illustrate the checks to do when merging
In [124]:
df_WAmod = df_WA[df_WA['ID'] != 'luca'].copy()
print(f"The command df_WAmod = df_WAmod[df_WAmod['ID'] != 'luca'].copy() creates a new DataFrame from df_WA by removing the row with ID 'luca':\n{df_WAmod}\n")
df_HAmod = df_HA[df_HA['ID'] != 'lynne'].copy()
print(f"The command df_HAmod = df_HA[df_HA['ID'] != 'lynne'].copy() creates a new DataFrame from df_HA by removing the row with ID 'lynne':\n{df_HAmod}\n")      

The command df_WAmod = df_WAmod[df_WAmod['ID'] != 'luca'].copy() creates a new DataFrame from df_WA by removing the row with ID 'luca':
        ID  weight  age
0      jin      60   11
2   mazhar      66   12
3    lynne      50   13
4  massimo      65   12
5  matthew      60   12

The command df_HAmod = df_HA[df_HA['ID'] != 'lynne'].copy() creates a new DataFrame from df_HA by removing the row with ID 'lynne':

3      jin     NaN   11
4  massimo   180.0   12
5   mazhar   175.0   12

Strategy for Effective Merging - Reindexing¶

  • Reindexing allows to use the method .index.get_level_values to get the keys
    • Not needed in our example with just one column for key
    • Convenient when there are multiple columns for the key

Strategy for Effective Merging - Reindexing¶

In [125]:
df_WAmod.set_index('ID', inplace=True)
print(f"The command df_WAmod.set_index('ID', inplace=True) sets the index of df_WAmod to 'ID':\n{df_WAmod}\n")
df_HAmod.set_index('ID', inplace=True)
print(f"The command df_HAmod.set_index('ID', inplace=True) sets the index of df_WAmod to 'ID':\n{df_HAmod}\n")

The command df_WAmod.set_index('ID', inplace=True) sets the index of df_WAmod to 'ID':

Strategy for Effective Merging - Identifying Non-Matching IDs/indexes/keys¶

  • In a MultiIndex, the get_level_values() method returns combinations of the index values at the specified level
    • This uniquely identifies each observation
    • Using a column is fine for a single key
    • With multiple IDs/indexes/keys it is better to use a MultiIndex

Strategy for Effective Merging - Identifying Non-Matching IDs/indexes/keys¶

In [126]:
idsReceiver_notIn_donor = set(df_WAmod.index.get_level_values('ID')) - set(df_HAmod.index.get_level_values('ID'))
print(f"""The command
idsReceiver_notIn_donor = set(df_WAmod.index.get_level_values('ID')) - set(df_HAmod.index.get_level_values('ID')) 
identifies unique IDs in df_WAmod (receiver) but not in df_HAmod (donor):\n
{idsReceiver_notIn_donor}""")

The command
idsReceiver_notIn_donor = set(df_WAmod.index.get_level_values('ID')) - set(df_HAmod.index.get_level_values('ID')) 
identifies unique IDs in df_WAmod (receiver) but not in df_HAmod (donor):

{'lynne'}
  • This check is in line with our expectations
    • No NaN arising due to typing differences or oddities due to duplicates
  • It identifiee the IDs that will result in NaN during the merge
    • These will be added to the ones already in the donor column

Strategy for Effective Merging - Merge the DataFrame one Column at a Time¶

  • Since we set the key column as index we can directly use join
In [127]:
df_WAmodJoined = df_WAmod.join(df_HAmod['height'])
print(f"""The command
df_WAmodJoined = df_WAmod.join(df_HAmod['height'])
adds the column 'height' from df_HAmod (donor) to df_WAmod (receiver) on the index:\n""")
df_WAmodJoined

The command
df_WAmodJoined = df_WAmod.join(df_HAmod['height'])
adds the column 'height' from df_HAmod (donor) to df_WAmod (receiver) on the index:

Strategy for Effective Merging - Compare the NaN Pre/Post Merge¶

  • We want to check the indexes of the NaN in:
    1. The column to be received (in the donor DataFrame)
    2. The column effectively received after merge (in the receiver DataFrame)
In [128]:
heightNan_idsDonor = set(df_HAmod[df_HAmod['height'].isna()].index.get_level_values('ID'))
print(f"""The command
heightNan_idsDonor = set(df_HAmod[df_HAmod['height'].isna()].index.get_level_values('ID')) 
stores the index of the NaN values in the 'height' column of the donor: \n{heightNan_idsDonor}\n""")
heightNan_idsReceived = set(df_WAmodJoined[df_WAmodJoined['height'].isna()].index.get_level_values('ID'))
print(f"""The command
heightNan_idsReceived = set(df_WAmodJoined[df_WAmodJoined['height'].isna()].index.get_level_values('ID'))
stores the indexes of the NaN values in the 'height' column received: \n{heightNan_idsReceived}""")

The command
heightNan_idsDonor = set(df_HAmod[df_HAmod['height'].isna()].index.get_level_values('ID')) 
stores the index of the NaN values in the 'height' column of the donor: 
{'jin'}

The command
heightNan_idsReceived = set(df_WAmodJoined[df_WAmodJoined['height'].isna()].index.get_level_values('ID'))
stores the indexes of the NaN values in the 'height' column received: 
{'lynne', 'jin'}

Strategy for Effective Merging - NaN Pre/Post Merge vs Non-Matching IDs/indexes/keys¶

  • We then compare the indexes with NaN in the received column (post merge) with the union of:
    1. The index of NaN in the column to be received (in the donor DataFrame)
    2. The non-matching IDs/indexes/keys
In [129]:
print(f"""The command
heightNan_idsReceived - (heightNan_idsDonor.union(idsReceiver_notIn_donor))
returns the IDs that are NaN in the receiver but not in the donor nor resulting from an IDs/indexes/keys mismatch:\n{heightNan_idsReceived - (heightNan_idsDonor.union(idsReceiver_notIn_donor))}""")

The command
heightNan_idsReceived - (heightNan_idsDonor.union(idsReceiver_notIn_donor))
returns the IDs that are NaN in the receiver but not in the donor nor resulting from an IDs/indexes/keys mismatch:
set()
  • In our example the result is an empty set
    • The merge went through as expected
